He says he cannot bring it himself, and names the eldest of the three children in Ruddedet's womb as the one who will.

kb.t: Atharvaveda (Bloomfield, Hymns of the Atharva-Veda)
kb.th: The Atharvaveda is the Veda of spells, made up of healing charms and hostile sorcery, and in Bloomfield's reading its witchcraft is part of religious thought, judged good or bad only by whom it is turned against.
h: A Brāhmaṇa passage presents yātu, sorcery, and those skilled in it as the representatives of the fourth Veda, and bheṣaja, healing charms, and yātu together make up what the name atharvāṅgirasaḥ embraces ([p. 26](/book/69907c2f5f855ec553e71f1b?page=26)).

The hostile hymns fall under the native classes ābhicārikāṇi, hostile rites, and kṛtyāpratiharaṇāni, rites that turn back a spell, and open with a call to Agni to make the sorcerers howl ([p. 144](/book/69907c2f5f855ec553e71f1b?page=144)).
The spell itself is addressed in the second person and threatened with having its neck and feet hewn off, with Indra and Agni called on to protect ([p. 155](/book/69907c2f5f855ec553e71f1b?page=155)).
Bloomfield concludes that witchcraft is blended with every sphere of religious thought and is judged useful or noxious only according to its target ([p. 43](/book/69907c2f5f855ec553e71f1b?page=43)).
tr: The text's own words divide the field into bheṣaja, healing, and yātu, abhicāra and kṛtyā, hostile sorcery; there is no single neutral word for magic, and the line falls by target and outcome, as Manu's law also rules for kṛtyā and abhicāra ([p. 26](/book/69907c2f5f855ec553e71f1b?page=26)); ([p. 144](/book/69907c2f5f855ec553e71f1b?page=144)); (p. 540).
an: Bloomfield's reading of the ritual texts, finding witchcraft accepted with no sign of repugnance, tells against Oldenberg's model of magic and sacrifice as two separate procedures that later mixed, and against Frazer-style magic and religion staging ([p. 43](/book/69907c2f5f855ec553e71f1b?page=43)).
Chinese Buddhist sources explained the Atharvaveda by 呪術, incantation, and by 禳災, averting calamity by prayer, the compound that later became the Japanese word for magic (p. 38).

He warns that Circe will cast drugs into the food, and that the remedy he gives will keep her from bewitching Odysseus. He instructs Odysseus to draw his sword when she strikes him with her wand, and to make her swear a great oath before he shares her bed.

Hippocratic Corpus, On the Sacred Diseas.a: The author argues that the sacred disease has a natural cause like other diseases, and that people call it divine because of inexperience and wonder. He reasons that anyone who could remove it by purification and magic could also bring it on by other arts, which would destroy the idea of divinity. He accuses such healers of pretending to know more than others and of deceiving people with cleansings and purifications.

q.t: For if they profess to know how to pull down the moon, to obscure the sun, to make storm and calm, rain and drought, and to render the sea or the land barren, and all other such things, whether they claim this power through sacred mysteries or some other expertise or practice, those who practice such things seem to me impious.

kb.t: Plato, Laws X–XI (on pharmakeia)
kb.th: Plato's Laws treats sorcery as a kind of poisoning that works through persuasion, and makes harmful spells a crime punished most severely in professional diviners.
h: Plato distinguishes two kinds of poisoning: harm done to the body by drugs, and harm by sorceries, incantations and spells that persuade both the doer and the victim of their power ([p. 467](/book/6953ce9377f38f6761be50b6?page=467)).
Plato holds it futile to tell suspicious people to ignore wax images found at doorways, crossroads or ancestors' tombs ([p. 467](/book/6953ce9377f38f6761be50b6?page=467)).
A prophet or diviner convicted of harm by bindings, incantations or spells is put to death, while a layman's penalty is left to the court ([p. 468](/book/6953ce9377f38f6761be50b6?page=468)).
tr: Plato's one word for poisoning covers both the drug and the spell, so the same term spans the poisoner and the sorcerer ([p. 467](/book/6953ce9377f38f6761be50b6?page=467)).
an: Apuleius cites Plato's account of Zalmoxis, that magical charms are merely beautiful words, in his own defence ([p. 54](/book/6953c71377f38f6761bda7f1?page=54)).
Apuleius accepts Plato's view that powers midway between gods and men control divination and the wonders of magicians ([p. 76](/book/6953c71377f38f6761bda7f1?page=76)).

kb.t: Theocritus, Idyll 2 (The Sorceress, Pharmakeutria)
kb.th: Theocritus' second Idyll shows a love rite that works by likeness, where what is done to an object is meant to happen to the beloved.
h: Simaetha's love rite works by likeness between the burning and melting objects and the man she wants ([p. 105](/book/69938e1dd5a98fd66f430715?page=105)).
As the laurel burns and the wax melts, so Delphis is meant to burn and melt with love ([p. 105](/book/69938e1dd5a98fd66f430715?page=105)).

1 Enoch, The Book of the Watchers (chs..a: In the Book of the Watchers, the angels who took wives taught them charms, enchantments, the cutting of roots and plants, and the text links this teaching to impiety, fornication and corruption. The Greek version assigns specific arts to named Watchers: Semyaza incantations and root-cutting, Armaros the releasing of charms, Kokabiel the signs, Sahiel star observation, and Seriel the courses of the moon. Azazel's teaching of metalwork, ornaments and dyes appears in the same lists, and the giants born of the unions devour mankind.

q.t: They began to go in to them and to defile themselves with them, and they taught them charms and enchantments, and the cutting of roots, and made them acquainted with plants.

Semyaza taught incantations and the cutting of roots [original: "ῥιζοτομίας"]. Armaros taught the releasing of charms; [gloss: Baraqiel taught astrology]. Kokabiel taught the signs; Sahiel taught the observation of stars [original: "ἀστεροσκοπίαν"].
From the 5th day to the 12th day, they shall dwell in the countryside.

The incantator [original: āšipu; a priest specializing in exorcism and protective magic.] and the kalû [original: kalû; the lamentation priest responsible for calming divine wrath through song.] shall reconcile this city.
"May the evil tongue stand aside." [original Akkadian: li-ša-nu li-mut-tu ina aḫâti lizsiz. This is a standard protective formula to ward off malicious speech or curses that could ruin the ritual.]

kb.t: Akītu (New Year) and kalû rituals of Uruk and Babylon
kb.th: These Babylonian temple rituals use incantation and purification to expel evil and demons from the temple at the New Year, performed by the temple's own incantation priest.
h: On the New Year festival the incantation priest (mašmašu) wipes the temple with a sheep's carcass and throws it into the river ([p. 151](/book/6992540ed5d1c6dbb2bcbcb8?page=151)).
After the purification the incantation priest stays outside Babylon from the 5th to the 12th day ([p. 151](/book/6992540ed5d1c6dbb2bcbcb8?page=151)).

The purification incantation names Marduk, Azag-sug and Nin-a-ha-du and drives all evil from the temple with the words 'O great demon, may Bêl destroy you!' ([p. 152](/book/6992540ed5d1c6dbb2bcbcb8?page=152)).
tr: The rites belong to the incantation priest (mašmašu), and calling this Babylonian temple exorcism 'magic' is said to be an outsider's label that should name whose word it is ([p. 151](/book/6992540ed5d1c6dbb2bcbcb8?page=151)); ([p. 55](/book/6953c71377f38f6761bda7f1?page=55)).

k.g: from Thessaly, a region associated with sorcery

Why do the gods trouble to heed these spells and herbs, and fear to despise them? What mutual bond puts constraint upon them? Must they obey, or do they take pleasure in obedience?
The profane spells of that ill-omened race compel the attention of the gods, who turn a deaf ear to so many peoples and nations.

kb.t: Lucan, Pharsalia VI (Erictho)
kb.th: Lucan's Erictho is the literary Thessalian witch whose power over the gods does not depend on prayer.
h: Erictho prays to no god above ([p. 358](/book/69af242c7c27d4b637fef7fa?page=358)).
The gods grant every crime she asks at the first word of her petition ([p. 358](/book/69af242c7c27d4b637fef7fa?page=358)).

Without doubt, it originated there in Persia with Zoroaster, as the authors agree. But whether this was one man, or another after him, is not sufficiently certain.

The first (as I find it) who wrote about it is Osthanes, who accompanied Xerxes, king of the Persians, in the war which he brought upon Greece; and he seems to have scattered the seeds of this monstrous art along the way
both arts flourished equally—I mean medicine and magic—at the same age, with Hippocrates illustrating the former, and Democritus the latter, around the time of the Peloponnesian War of Greece.

kb.t: Pliny the Elder, Natural History XXX (the history of magic)
kb.th: Pliny calls magic the most fraudulent of arts, a foreign import from Persia that holds mankind because it absorbed medicine, religion and astrology.
h: Magic holds people because it took over three other arts: medicine, religion and astrology ([p. 240](/book/69b00f46f0043345da7679a6?page=240)).

Magic began in Persia with Zoroaster, and Osthanes, who came with Xerxes' invasion, spread the 'monstrous art' among the Greeks ([p. 241](/book/69b00f46f0043345da7679a6?page=241)); ([p. 242](/book/69b00f46f0043345da7679a6?page=242)).
Pliny says Pythagoras, Empedocles, Democritus and Plato sailed abroad to learn magic and kept it among their secrets on their return ([p. 242](/book/69b00f46f0043345da7679a6?page=242)).
He counts the Druids of Gaul, the rites of Britain and a Jewish faction under Moses, Jannes and Jotape as branches of the same magic ([p. 243](/book/69b00f46f0043345da7679a6?page=243)).
Nero, with unlimited wealth and desire, studied magic and found it vain and false, which Pliny treats as the decisive test ([p. 244](/book/69b00f46f0043345da7679a6?page=244)).
tr: Pliny's 'magic' is said to be an accuser's term for foreign priesthoods and practices, so his history is a hostile genealogy written from outside ([p. 55](/book/6953c71377f38f6761bda7f1?page=55)).

it is absolutely necessary that his name be inscribed on the plate; otherwise the formulas fall void or perhaps recoil upon the one performing the curse.
You will not deny that the divine name Iao lies hidden under iaoth and ioth.

kb.t: Curse tablets (defixiones), in Audollent, Defixionum tabellae
kb.th: The curse tablets bind a named victim, whether a legal opponent or a desired woman, by writing the name on lead and handing it to underworld or secret powers.
h: The victim's name had to be written on the tablet, or the formula failed or recoiled on the curser ([p. 64](/book/6a3f01fe661123baf6fe996d?page=64)).
Lead was chosen either as Saturn's deathly metal, fit for a deadly work, or simply because it was convenient to write on ([p. 64](/book/6a3f01fe661123baf6fe996d?page=64)).
An Attic tablet consigns a group of legal adversaries to Hermes katochos, 'the binder' ([p. 248](/book/6a3f01fe661123baf6fe996d?page=248)).

A Latin love curse in Greek letters from Hadrumetum asks secret powers to make Tottina love the writer, with the divine name Iao hidden in its barbarous names ([p. 523](/book/6a3f01fe661123baf6fe996d?page=523)).

Audollent sets beside the tablets the Great Paris papyrus's love binding, made with two wax figures: an armed male like Ares and a bound, kneeling female carrying the woman's hair ([p. 99](/book/6a3f01fe661123baf6fe996d?page=99)).

Plutarch, On the Obsolescence of Oracles.a: Cleombrotus and the other speakers place daimones between gods and humans as a medium that joins the two. Xenocrates, as reported, compares the isosceles triangle to the daimonic nature, which has "both the passion of the mortal and the power of the god." The speakers cite Hesiod's four races (gods, good daimones, heroes, humans) and a view that better souls change from humans to heroes to daimones, with a few purified wholly into divinity, while others re-enter mortal bodies.

q.t: He compared the equilateral triangle to the divine, the scalene to the mortal, and the isosceles to the daimonic spirit-like. The first is equal in every way, the second unequal in every way, and the third is equal in some ways and unequal in others, just like the nature of daimones, which possesses both the passion of the mortal and the power of the god.

Others posit a transformation for bodies and souls alike, just as water is seen being generated from earth, air from water, and fire from air, as the substance is carried upward. In this way, better souls take their transformation from humans into heroes, and from heroes into daimones.

Kauṭilya, Arthaśāstra (Book 14, secret p.a: Book 14 is headed the Aupanishadika, Secret/Occult Knowledge, and its chapter on medicinal and mantric operations pairs mantra with medicine against enemies. Elsewhere Kautilya has spies pose as holy men with door-opening, invisibility, sleep-inducing and attraction mantras to trap thieves. He also has agents stage divine signs, and directs the king to honor magicians and to use Atharvaveda rites against demons.

q.t: Its application: On the dark fourteenth day, after the porcupine quills have been kept for seven nights, one should perform a fire sacrifice with Khadira Acacia catechu wood, chanting this mantra one hundred and eight times, and offer honey and ghee. Then, if one buries one quill at the village gate or the house gate using this mantra, it puts everything there to sleep.

Then, using the "door-opening" mantra, they should open the doors and say, "Enter." Using the "invisibility" mantra, they should lead the youths through the middle of the watchful guards. Using the "sleep-inducing" mantra, they should put them to sleep and move the youths through the quarters of the guards.

Therefore, the king should honor and provide a place to live in his kingdom for those holy men who are experts in the magical arts and possess the supernatural powers required to turn away disasters sent by fate.

And one of these teaches the boy the magic of Zoroaster the son of Oromazes; and this magic is no other than the worship of the gods.

kb.t: Apuleius, Apology (De magia)
kb.th: Apuleius, on trial for magic, argues that 'magus' properly means a Persian priest and that philosophers are routinely and wrongly called magicians, so the charge is the ignorant accuser's label.
h: Apuleius cites authors who say 'magus' is the Persian word for priest, and Plato's account that the magic of Zoroaster is the worship of the gods ([p. 53](/book/6953c71377f38f6761bda7f1?page=53)).
He names Epimenides, Orpheus, Pythagoras and Ostanes as philosophers whom the uninitiated wrongly called magicians ([p. 55](/book/6953c71377f38f6761bda7f1?page=55)).
He answers the charge of buying fish by saying he sought remedies in them, as a doctor or philosopher would ([p. 72](/book/6953c71377f38f6761bda7f1?page=72)).

He accepts Plato's view that powers midway between gods and men control all divination and the miracles of magicians ([p. 76](/book/6953c71377f38f6761bda7f1?page=76)); ([p. 21](/book/6990633bef12272ffdc90769?page=21)).
He argues that his wife's letter calling him a magician cannot by itself prove the charge ([p. 149](/book/69af217f7c27d4b637fed9e0?page=149)).
tr: Apuleius sets the learned sense of magus, a Persian priest, against the common sense of a magician who works any marvel by speaking with the gods, and turns the common sense against his accusers ([p. 53](/book/6953c71377f38f6761bda7f1?page=53)); ([p. 54](/book/6953c71377f38f6761bda7f1?page=54)).
The speech is said to show 'magic' as an accuser's word, applied to philosophers and pious men ([p. 55](/book/6953c71377f38f6761bda7f1?page=55)).
an: Thorndike reads the speech as hinting that Roman law condemned magic only on proof of harm or unjust gain ([p. 281](/book/699069212f82e0fda4804270?page=281)).
Butler and Owen reply that the Twelve Tables already forbade magic and that the lex Cornelia covered all magic practised for evil ends ([p. 176](/book/69af217f7c27d4b637fed9e0?page=176)).
A 1572 commentary on the Twelve Tables quotes Apuleius that magic was forbidden there for incantations against crops (p. 22).

Apuleius, On the God of Socrates (De deo.a: Apuleius places the daimones in the air between the highest aether and the earth, since a god never communicates with a man directly. He assigns each a province, such as confirming dreams, inspecting entrails, governing birds of omen, inspiring prophets and hurling lightnings. These act by the will of the heavenly ones, and he cites the omens given to Hannibal, Flaminius and Accius Navius. He also sorts the human soul into genius, lemur, lar familiaris, larua and Manes.

k.g: a guiding spirit or intermediate being
ghosts or spirits of the dead

q.t: They are carriers between mortals and the inhabitants of heaven, carrying prayers from here and gifts from there, carrying petitions from here and aid from there, like certain interpreters and bringers of health on both sides. Through these same ones, as Plato asserts in the Symposium Plato's dialogue on love, all announcements and the various miracles of the magi and all types of omens are ruled.

In a second sense, the human soul is a species of daemon when it is stripped and free, having renounced the duties of life and left its body. I find that in the old Latin language, this was called a lemur spirit of the dead.

Apuleius, Metamorphoses (The Golden Ass).a: Byrrhena warns Lucius that Pamphile, wife of his host Milo, is believed to be a sorceress of the first rank and mistress of every sepulchral incantation. She is said to breathe upon twigs and pebbles and sink the light of the stars into Tartarus and ancient chaos. Byrrhena says Pamphile binds handsome youths with love and turns those who displease her into stones, cattle or other animals, or destroys them. Lucius, who had always desired the magic art, longs to submit to her.

q.t: She is believed to be a sorceress of the first rank, and a mistress of every sepulchral incantation, who, by breathing upon twigs and pebbles and frivolous things of that sort, knows how to submerge all this light of the starry world into the depths of Tartarus and into ancient chaos.

as is the name Seraphim, Cherubim, Michael, Gabriel. For thus, pronounced according to the dialect of the Hebrews, they have a singular and ineffable efficacy in the administration of sacred things; but when changed into Greek names, they are entirely powerless.

As far as I am concerned, I do not approve of the sacred rites of the Chaldeans at all, nor do I assent to their doctrine. With difficulty, however, I have uncovered the obscurity of the oracle for you.

Pliny recounts that medicine [original: "Medicina"] was the third part of magic. But we, together with great and pious men, say that magic embraces the knowledge of the whole of nature [original: "natura"] universally.

kb.t: Chaldaean Oracles
kb.th: The Oracles are the scripture of theurgy, and their best-known rule holds that barbarous sacred names must never be changed, since their power lies in the original words.
h: One oracle forbids changing the barbarous names used in rites ([p. 96](/book/69b51ebdff09e4fe943b3e60?page=96)).
As Psellos explains it, names such as Seraphim, Cherubim, Michael and Gabriel carry an ineffable efficacy in Hebrew and lose it when put into Greek ([p. 96](/book/69b51ebdff09e4fe943b3e60?page=96)).
an: Iamblichus holds the same doctrine, that the sacred names cannot be translated without losing their power ([p. 328](/book/69d149ce1c2a66dc094b30c3?page=328)).
Psellos expounds the Oracles while saying he approves neither their rites nor their doctrine ([p. 96](/book/69b51ebdff09e4fe943b3e60?page=96)).

Augustine takes Porphyry's story of a Chaldaean whose rite was frustrated by a rival's binding as proof that theurgy works for evil as well as good ([p. 236](/book/699062f5ef12272ffdc8e9d5?page=236)).

Lucian, The Lover of Lies (Philopseudes).a: The speakers report healings and feats by named practitioners. A Chaldean from Babylon cures the viper-bitten Midas with an incantation and a stone chipped from a tombstone, and chants seven divine and demonic names from an ancient book. Ion describes a Syrian from Palestine who questions a possessed man's demon, hears it answer in Greek or a foreign tongue, and drives it out with oaths and threats. A Hyperborean magician is said to raise spirits and corpses, summon Hecate, and draw down the moon, and he digs a trench at midnight to call up the dead Anaxicles for a fee. The narrator doubts the magician's price and motives.

q.t: For when he stands over the ones lying there and asks whence they have entered the body, the sick man himself is silent, but the demon answers, either speaking Greek or a foreign language, or from wherever he happens to be, and from where he came into the man. And he, by using oaths, and if they do not obey, by threats, drives the demon out.

And so that I do not spend time talking, the Babylonian came, and he healed Midas, driving out the venom from his body with a certain incantation, and even attaching to his foot a stone from a fallen rock, having chipped it from a tombstone.

For what is the need even to speak of these small things, how many he displayed, sending up spirits, and raising demons, and calling up stale corpses, and bringing Hecate herself to appear clearly, and drawing down the moon.

Irenaeus, Against Heresies I (Simon Magu.a: Irenaeus presents Simon the Samaritan as a magus who seduced the Samaritans and who took the Apostles' healings for magic, offering them money for the power of giving the Holy Spirit. The followers of Simon are said to practice exorcisms, incantations, love potions, familiar spirits (paredri) and dream-senders (oniropompi). They also keep an image of Simon in the likeness of Jupiter and one of Helena as Minerva, and they adore these.

q.t: Therefore, the mystical priests of these men live indeed licentiously, but they perform magic arts, as each of them is able. They use exorcisms and incantations. Love potions and charms, and what are called paredri and oniropompi (dream-senders), and whatever other perierga (curious arts) exist, are diligently practiced among them.
This is the power of God, which is called great. And they gave heed to him, because that for a long time he had bewitched them with his magical arts.

Corpus Hermeticum (Poimandres and the Gr.a: Trismegistus tells Asclepius of animated statues, full of sense and spirit, that foresee the future, predict through dreams, and inflict and cure illnesses according to merit. He calls Egypt the image of heaven and the earth the temple of the whole world. He foretells that divinity will return to heaven, foreigners will fill Egypt, and religion and divine worship will be forbidden by law under penalty.

q.t: I speak of animated statues, full of sense and spirit, which do such great and many things. Statues that foresee the future, and perhaps predict it by means of dreams and many other things; statues that inflict illnesses upon men and cure them, granting sadness or joy according to merit.

The Halakhas of witchcraft are similar to the Halakhas of Sabbath. There are some to which stoning applies; there are some which are not allowed to start with, but if, nevertheless, one has done them, he is free; and some are allowed even to start with.
Said Abayi: A conjurer who is particular to use a utensil, it is by a demon, and he who is not particular, it is by witchcraft.
To dazzle the eyes is not allowed to start with, but if one did, he is free. And it is allowed to start with, as said above. R. Hanina and R. Oshia were accustomed to create a calf, etc.

kb.t: Mishnah and Talmud, Sanhedrin (the law on kishuf)
kb.th: Rabbinic law makes sorcery a capital crime only when a real deed is done, and grades the rest like Sabbath law, from stoning down to the permitted.
h: The capital sorcerer (mekhashef) is one who performs an actual deed, not one who merely produces an illusion (Mishnah Sanhedrin 7:11); ([p. 796](/book/69920befebe5b0fa6be5d569?page=796)).

The Talmud grades witchcraft like Sabbath law: some acts incur stoning, some are forbidden but unpunished, and some are permitted from the outset (Sanhedrin 67b); ([p. 227](/book/69ad70eac5001c07fa846ae5?page=227)).
Abaye tells an effect worked through a demon from one worked by witchcraft by whether the practitioner insists on a specific utensil ([p. 227](/book/69ad70eac5001c07fa846ae5?page=227)).
Deceiving the eyes is forbidden but unpunished, while rabbis who regularly created a calf are the example of what is permitted from the outset ([p. 227](/book/69ad70eac5001c07fa846ae5?page=227)).
tr: The law's word kishuf names a real deed punished with death, and English 'magic' covers both it and the lesser 'seizing of the eyes', which the law forbids without punishing ([p. 796](/book/69920befebe5b0fa6be5d569?page=796)); ([p. 227](/book/69ad70eac5001c07fa846ae5?page=227)).
an: Lea (1888) argues that rabbinic Judaism enforced the witch law relentlessly, citing Simeon ben Shetach's hanging of eighty 'witches' at Ascalon; the Mishnah is said to call them 'women' and to have the Sages flag the act as irregular ([p. 412](/book/699069572f82e0fda48071b4?page=412)); ([p. 790](/book/69920befebe5b0fa6be5d569?page=790)).

Eisenmenger (1711) quotes the Talmud that two rabbis studied the Book of Yetzirah every Sabbath eve and created a three-year-old calf, and reports the Jewish view that powerful things are done by arranging its letters (p. 538).
A 1668 Latin commentary reads Maimonides' law as separating demonic magic, punished by stoning, from sleight of hand, punished by lashes ([p. 168](/book/69c89ffe6c6f3cc53c85deb7?page=168)).

Philostratus, Life of Apollonius of Tyan.a: In the 1504 Latin edition the narrator answers those who call Apollonius a student of the magic art because he stayed with the Magi, Brahmins and Gymnosophists. He points to Empedocles, Pythagoras, Democritus and Plato, who also visited such teachers and were not suspected of magic. In the defence speech, Apollonius says he foresaw the plague at Ephesus because of his light diet, and compares his foreknowledge with the daimonion of Socrates. The Indian sage Iarchas gives him seven rings named after the seven stars, and Apollonius is said to have written on astrological divination and on sacrifices.

q.t: There are even those who proclaim him to be most studious of the magic art, because he had spent time in Babylonia with the Magi, in India with the Brahmins, and in Egypt with the Gymnosophists; and they slander him for this very reason, that he attained his wisdom, as it were, by some violence—not indeed thinking correctly about such a man.

He claims this is beyond wisdom and is miraculous, and that I could not have reached such a level of truth if I were not a wizard and an unspeakable wretch. What, then, will Socrates say here regarding the things he claimed to learn from his divine spirit daimonion?

But I believe that the science of the stars and the entire art of divination exceed the limits of human nature, and whether anyone truly knows it, I do not know. Regarding the performing of sacrifices, however, I have found many writings in many temples, and I have also found them publicly in some cities and in the private homes of wise men.

Hippolytus, Refutation of All Heresies I.a: Hippolytus explains how a sorcerer reads a question written in water: he burns a decoy paper with Cyphi incense, cries out to a demon named Phryn, and revives the hidden letters with a copperas mixture. He also describes a closed room with a blue ceiling reflected in a cauldron of water, accomplices dressed as gods, and a burning demon drawn with asphalt. He says he published these methods to protect young people and to shame the magicians.

q.t: The sorcerer takes a paper and directs the inquirer to write down with water whatever questions he wishes to ask the demons. Then, folding the paper and handing it to an attendant, he sends him away to cast it into the flames so that the rising smoke may carry the letters to the demons.

Even if one person uses this information to learn evil, another person will, by being instructed in these tricks, be preserved from them. Furthermore, the magicians themselves—those corrupters of life—will be ashamed when their art is exposed.

The magician plunges his hands into the "boiling" pitch, but he has actually thrown vinegar, soda [original: natron.], and moist pitch into the cauldron and heated it gently. The vinegar reacting with the soda causes the pitch to bubble, creating the appearance of boiling.
