He says that within the soul of man there exists a certain power of changing things [original: "virtus immutandi res"], and that other things are obedient to it when the soul itself is carried away into a great excess of love, or of hatred, or of some such emotion. Therefore, when the soul of someone is carried into a great onset of any passion, it is found by manifest experiment that the soul itself binds things.

kb.t: Pseudo-Albertus Magnus, The Book of Secrets (Liber aggregationis)
kb.th: The Book of Secrets holds that magical science is good to know, and only its use can be bad; it collects the occult virtues of herbs, stones and animals as practical recipes.
h: Magical science is not bad in itself, since knowing it lets one avoid evil and pursue good; only its use can be bad ([p. 5](/book/69dbc52637db7bc4b2eb262d?page=5)).
Its recipes give herbs occult effects, such as celandine carried with a mole's heart to defeat enemies and win lawsuits ([p. 6](/book/69dbc52637db7bc4b2eb262d?page=6)).
The pseudo-Albertine secrets report that a drum of wolfskin silences one of sheepskin (p. 280).
an: Agrippa takes the wolf-drum secret as proof that antipathy acts through sound as well as touch, adding that wolf-gut and sheep-gut strings on one lyre make no consonance (p. 280).

Bruno explains the wolf drum by the spirit left in the dead skin mastering the sheep's spirit, admits he has not tested it, and suggests an ass-skin drum might win merely by being thicker ([p. 513](/book/69905e232fd6a039938a1235?page=513)).
A 1688 dissertation on the wolf follows Gesner in explaining the drum naturally: harder wolf skin simply sounds clearer and lasts longer, with no occult enmity needed (p. 36).

kb.t: Pseudo-Albertus Magnus, The Marvels of the World (De mirabilibus mundi)
kb.th: The Marvels of the World grounds magic in the human soul: a soul carried into great passion can change and bind outside things, and this is why words and characters made at such a moment work.
h: Following Avicenna, the human soul carried into great excess of love, hatred or another passion has a power that changes and binds external things ([p. 190](/book/6988a59f8f2b65d11145d732?page=190)).
The author says he long disbelieved this binding power until he read books of necromancy ([p. 190](/book/6988a59f8f2b65d11145d732?page=190)).

A greater excess of the soul always binds, prevents or dissolves a lesser one, so characters and spoken words made in the hour of the operator's strongest desire are effective ([p. 6](/book/69dbc79d1040d1d5e2092e0e?page=6)).

out of 89 masters gathered from Naples, Athens, and Toledo, we selected one named Honorius, son of Euclid, master of Thebes … so-called because the hundred sacred names of God are included in this book
that it shall be copied by no more than three; and that it shall be given to no woman, nor to any man unless he be of mature age, very honest, and faithful
The centerpiece of the text is the ritual to attain nothing less than the beatific vision.

kb.t: Sworn Book of Honorius (Liber iuratus)
kb.th: The Sworn Book presents itself as a sacred book of magic, made holy by the hundred names of God, whose central rite aims at the beatific vision.
h: Its frame story has pope and cardinals, stirred by demons, declare that salvation is being turned to damnation through magic and nigromancy ([p. 50](/book/6959359d3b43cb6630c913d9?page=50)).

A council of 89 masters from Naples, Athens and Toledo chose Honorius of Thebes to condense seven volumes of magic into one book, called sacred or sworn because it holds the hundred sacred names of God ([p. 52](/book/6959359d3b43cb6630c913d9?page=52)).
Its oath allows at most three copies, never to a woman, and only to a mature, honest and faithful man after a year's testing ([p. 51](/book/6959359d3b43cb6630c913d9?page=51)).

Its modern editor identifies the centerpiece as a ritual to attain the beatific vision, followed by rites using prayers, conjurations, seals, swords, circles and the names of God, angels and demons ([p. 15](/book/6959359d3b43cb6630c913d9?page=15)).
an: Thorndike judged the proemium's council of magicians against pope and prelates 'probably more impressive than true', a legend rather than history ([p. 299](/book/699069252f82e0fda48046c3?page=299)).

kb.t: Nicole Oresme, On the Causes of Marvels (De causis mirabilium)
kb.th: Oresme gives natural causes for marvels, and explains apparitions of the dead as the work of a strong imagination rather than of spirits.
h: A mourner's strong fantasy of a dead father can make him take a staff or a shadow for the father, so the apparition has a natural cause ([p. 20](/book/6978ee36a87012956d883ad2?page=20)).

Claudius Coelestinus, who wrote on marvels along Oresme's lines, holds that the existence of demons cannot be proven by natural reason and must be believed by faith alone ([p. 50](/book/69af1366199e32dea75fa181?page=50)).
an: Claudius Coelestinus says his treatise on marvels in nature (French, 1557) follows Oresme almost word for word, while disagreeing with him on celestial influences ([p. 134](/book/6978ee36a87012956d883ad2?page=134)).

The prophetic soul, according to them, has essential properties, among which is the issuing of these supernatural events by his power and the obedience of the elements to him in creation.
they cling to partial, sensory, or imagined matters, such as transparent bodies, animal bones, rhymed speech, or whatever may occur of birds or animals.

kb.t: Ibn Khaldūn, Muqaddima, ch. 6 (on sorcery and talismans)
kb.th: Ibn Khaldūn holds that sorcery is real and rests on a power of the soul, ranks its kinds, and separates it from the prophet's miracle and the saint's wonder.
h: The prophetic miracle differs from a saint's karāma and from sorcery by the challenge the prophet issues in advance ([p. 182](/book/69e8b29f2ff2a8dc09e78458?page=182)).
Macdonald reports his view that magicians have an inborn psychic power to influence things and draw down the spiritual force of the stars ([p. 135](/book/699079397d066daf3b4a93d8?page=135)).

Macdonald reports that he ranked three kinds of magic, by the soul alone, by aid of spheres, elements and numbers (the weaker talismanic art), and by working on the imagination, and held the first two certainly real, citing the Qurʾān on Hārūt and Mārūt and the blowers on knots ([p. 136](/book/699079397d066daf3b4a93d8?page=136)); ([p. 137](/book/699079397d066daf3b4a93d8?page=137)).
He is said to have watched a sorcerer make a figure of the victim, knot a cord and blow on it, an evil spirit going out with the saliva ([p. 138](/book/699079397d066daf3b4a93d8?page=138)).

Geomancy is allowed only as a way to occupy the senses so the soul turns to the spiritual world, and as a technique for knowing the unseen it is nonsense ([p. 222](/book/69e8b29f2ff2a8dc09e78458?page=222)); ([p. 220](/book/69e8b29f2ff2a8dc09e78458?page=220)).
tr: His siḥr is one of three terms for wonders, set against the prophet's miracle (muʿjiza) and the saint's karāma, and the line between them is drawn by a theologian, by who works the wonder and how it is announced ([p. 182](/book/69e8b29f2ff2a8dc09e78458?page=182)).

q.t: After the fourth pull of the ropes … 'I procure hailstorms easily, but I am not able to cause harm at my own whim; I can only hurt those who are destitute of God's help. Those who arm themselves with the sign of the cross will not perish by my lightning.'
First, with specific words in a field, we implore the prince of all demons to send one of his followers to strike the place we have designated.
Attack the wretch with confidence, because once he is touched by public justice … he will lose all the strength of his wickedness.

kb.t: Johannes Nider, The Anthill (Formicarius)
kb.th: Through a judge's trial reports, Nider presents weather-making sorcery as a real power worked through demons, limited by God's protection and broken by public justice.
h: Nider reports the judge Peter's account that Stadelein, after four pulls of the strappado, said he raised hail easily but could not harm those armed with the sign of the cross ([p. 397](/book/699052328d19cbc90d9d55f6?page=397)).
In the same confession, weather-making begins with set words spoken in a field to implore the prince of demons to send one of his followers ([p. 397](/book/699052328d19cbc90d9d55f6?page=397)).

Nider's judge holds that a sorcerer loses all power once touched by public justice, and orders his frightened servants to seize Stadelein on that ground ([p. 397](/book/699052328d19cbc90d9d55f6?page=397)).
an: Reginald Scot denies that witches or devils can command the elements or send rain, hail and storms, naming Nider in the margin ([p. 143](/book/695926cc15b4070cb1e80050?page=143)).

Hygromanteia (Magical Treatise of Solomo.a: Solomon tells Roboam to name the angels and the ruling demons of each planet for its day and hour. An exorcism of the angels asks them to subject the demons of that hour, and the Sun is given five angels and three demons. The exorcism texts adjure evil demons by archangels, by the four pillars of fire called sorcery-dissolvers, and by the Trinity, and they list many kinds of demon, including the demon of sorcery. In the Solomon narrative a boy holding the Seal of God commands demons in the name of the Lord God Most High.

k.g: a method of divination using a water-filled vessel

kb.t: Munich Necromancer's Handbook (Clm 849)
kb.th: The Munich Handbook treats necromancy as the command of spirits by names, ring, sword and circle, able to produce visions seen by the operator alone.
h: Spirits are commanded by lists of strange names and by a ring to leave their places at once ([p. 20](/book/69905e292fd6a039938a15c6?page=20)).

One operation prescribes a polished sword and a hoopoe, circles traced with the sword in a remote place on Sunday at noon, and sixteen names written with its edge ([p. 30](/book/69905e292fd6a039938a15c6?page=30)).

One experiment narrates in the first person a spirit appearing as a noble soldier, visible only to the operator, who promises to produce a legion of spirits as was once shown to an emperor ([p. 40](/book/69905e292fd6a039938a15c6?page=40)).

kb.t: Giovanni Pico della Mirandola, Oration on the Dignity of Man
kb.th: Pico divides magic in two: one kind is wholly the work of demons and execrable, and the other is the absolute perfection of natural philosophy, in which the magus serves nature as she works her wonders.
h: Magic is twofold, one kind the work of demons, 'execrable and monstrous', the other nothing but the absolute perfection of natural philosophy ([p. 360](/book/6952b03577f38f6761bc211a?page=360)).
Citing Plotinus, Pico calls the magus the servant of nature and holds that natural magic diligently serves nature as she works wonders ([p. 155](/book/6952b03577f38f6761bc211a?page=155)).

Good magic comes from Zoroaster, whose magic is the science of divine things, and Zamolxis, whose magic is medicine of the soul, and its recent heirs include al-Kindi, Roger Bacon and William of Paris ([p. 155](/book/6952b03577f38f6761bc211a?page=155)).
tr: Pico says the Greeks do not dignify the demonic kind with the name of magic and call it goeteia, keeping mageia for the highest knowledge; after Porphyry he glosses magus as the Persian for 'interpreter and worshipper of divine things' (p. 91).
an: Martius (1717) likewise takes the Greek ho Magos to mean a knowing or wise man, set apart from Luke's Zauberer and the black, diabolical art (p. 24).

kb.t: Giovanni Pico della Mirandola, The 900 Conclusions and the Apology
kb.th: Pico holds that natural magic, as part of natural science, together with Kabbalah gives the greatest certainty of any human science and best certifies the divinity of Christ.
h: The Apologia defends the thesis that no science more certifies Christ's divinity than magic and Kabbalah, saying the censors must accept its affirmative form as Catholic ([p. 130](/book/adad5f6d-4f68-4009-9406-d0e083cf0acc?page=130)).

No humanly discovered science gives greater certainty than the magic of the conclusions, which Pico makes part of natural science, and the scientific part of Kabbalah ([p. 201](/book/6952b03577f38f6761bc211a?page=201)).
Pico rejects the superstitious and diabolical kind of magic and approves the natural kind ([p. 205](/book/6952b03577f38f6761bc211a?page=205)).
Among the conclusions, formal arithmetic is the best way to natural prophecy, and through numbers a way is had to understanding every knowable thing (p. 132).
tr: Pico argues that 'Magus' should not always be heard as 'worshipper of demons', since the Persian Magi were philosophers and not necromancers ([p. 205](/book/6952b03577f38f6761bc211a?page=205)).
an: The examining masters called the thesis on magic and Kabbalah false, erroneous and heretical ([p. 201](/book/6952b03577f38f6761bc211a?page=201)).
Ginsburg (1865) reports that Pico found more Christianity than Judaism in the Kabbalah, which led to the 900 Theses and the thesis on magic and Kabbalah (p. 134).

kb.t: Heinrich Kramer, The Hammer of Witches (Malleus maleficarum)
kb.th: The Malleus treats witchcraft as a heresy worked through the meeting of demon, witch and divine permission, and holds that denying witches exist may itself be heretical.
h: Written after Innocent VIII's bull, it frames a work of witchcraft as the meeting of demon, witch and divine permission, and first asks whether denying witches is heretical ([p. 7](/book/69523495ab34727b1f044a45?page=7)).

It argues that more women than men are infected by the heresy of witches, names the heresy in the feminine for that reason, and thanks God for preserving the male sex ([p. 49](/book/69523495ab34727b1f044a45?page=49)).
It allows death only on confession, manifest proof or witnesses, and sends the accused to interrogation and torture for confession ([p. 214](/book/69523495ab34727b1f044a45?page=214)).
It sets the heresy of the malefici apart from simple heresies, which involve no pact, and ranks it highest in malice among all kinds of divination ([p. 60](/book/69bd9c796120d54bd036f318?page=60)).
tr: The Malleus derives the name of the malefici 'from evil-doing or from thinking ill of the faith', so its word for the practitioner is the accuser's word for a heretic bound by a pact ([p. 60](/book/69bd9c796120d54bd036f318?page=60)).
an: The historian Joseph Hansen reports that Sprenger, with Institoris, obtained the bull Summis desiderantes affectibus of 5 December 1484, which led to the Malleus of 1486, a book Hansen attributes to Institoris ([p. 417](/book/69905e1a2fd6a039938a0f5d?page=417)).

kb.t: Marsilio Ficino, Three Books on Life (De vita libri tres)
kb.th: Ficino presents magic as a part of natural philosophy: the world breathes a spirit, and the souls of the world, the stars and demons can be drawn into suitably prepared bodies, so that celestial power is brought down into earthly things.
h: The world lives and breathes, and a man draws its spirit in through his own spirit, which is by nature conformable to it ([p. 166](/book/69906831249ce014347d5b5c?page=166)).

Ficino says he reports the astronomical images more than he approves them, and he sets Aquinas's view that figures gain only the common power of the heavens against Peter of Abano's claim that an image destroyed a region ([p. 150](/book/69906831249ce014347d5b5c?page=150)); ([p. 239](/book/69906831249ce014347d5b5c?page=239)).

He refuses to give the details of a Moon-Venus love image ('we are not teaching love charms, but medicines') and ascribes such effects, and any speaking statues, to deceiving daemons ([p. 251](/book/69906831249ce014347d5b5c?page=251)); ([p. 283](/book/69906831249ce014347d5b5c?page=283)).

A song made with the right virtue, timing and intention is 'another spirit' that draws the celestial influx and can cure diseases of mind and body ([p. 159](/book/69dbc9fe1040d1d5e20a8528?page=159)); (p. 388).

Ficino reports that a person's Daemon is usually held to depend on the lord of the birth chart, the 'good Daemon' descending from the eleventh house ([p. 167](/book/69dbc9fe1040d1d5e20a8528?page=167)).
tr: Ficino's magus is the philosopher skilled in natural things and the stars, who inserts celestial things into terrestrial ones by allurements as a farmer grafts a shoot onto old stock ([p. 280](/book/69906831249ce014347d5b5c?page=280)).
an: Agrippa gives every person three guardian daemons and assigns the sacred one to the soul by God, the ruler of daemons, apart from the stars ([p. 483](/book/698420e1f1fb376a3d58061c?page=483)).

kb.t: Key of Solomon (Clavicula Salomonis)
kb.th: The Key of Solomon presents ritual magic as the celestial science Solomon handed down to his son Rehoboam, worked through Hebrew divine names written on virgin parchment.
h: The French Key claims descent from a Hebrew original, translated into Latin by Rabbi Abognazar, carried to Arles, and put into French by the Archbishop Barrault after the expulsion of the Jews ([p. 5](/book/69592f6ca41e40e9146a45d7?page=5)).
It opens with Solomon telling Rehoboam that no science is 'more natural or more useful than the knowledge of the Celestial movements' ([p. 5](/book/69592f6ca41e40e9146a45d7?page=5)).

It lists ten Hebrew divine names, among them Ehieh, Elohim, Shaddai and Shekinah, which, written on virgin lambskin parchment and carried, will 'acquire for you great prosperity' ([p. 34](/book/69592f6ca41e40e9146a45d7?page=34)).
An eighteenth-century French manuscript of the Keys opens by asserting that Solomon possessed the 'infused sciences' through an angel's teachings ([p. 9](/book/69b418b52b0edf3eaa2ddb30?page=9)).
an: Waite (1898) reported the Key in Latin, French, Italian and German manuscripts, the oldest used by Mathers being sixteenth-century Latin, and found the claim of a Hebrew original not 'essentially improbable' ([p. 81](/book/69c896426c6f3cc53c85c4ea?page=81)).

Waite also named back-dating and imputed authorship as 'the two crying bibliographical sins of Grimoires', which tells against taking the Solomonic attribution at face value ([p. 49](/book/69c896426c6f3cc53c85c4ea?page=49)).

kb.t: Pseudo-Peter of Abano, Heptameron, or Magical Elements
kb.th: The Heptameron is a working manual of planetary-day conjuration, giving the circle, angel names and spirits of the air for each day, and it presents itself as an introduction for beginners.
h: It is printed after the Fourth Book on the stated ground that the Fourth Book treated ceremonies only in general, for the learned ([p. 89](/book/695234e3ab34727b1f044dc2?page=89)).
Its own preface describes the book as 'a certain introduction of Magical vanity' for those who 'have not tasted of Magical Superstitions' ([p. 90](/book/695234e3ab34727b1f044dc2?page=90)).

It holds that the form of the circle changes with the spirits called, their places, times, days and hours, and prescribes three circles nine feet across ([p. 90](/book/695234e3ab34727b1f044dc2?page=90)).

Its Sunday conjuration adjures Michael, 'chief Ruler of the Lords day', by divine names and by the Sun, and the Sunday spirits of the air procure gold, gems and riches ([p. 110](/book/695234e3ab34727b1f044dc2?page=110)).

kb.t: Johannes Trithemius, Antipalus maleficiorum
kb.th: Trithemius treats magic as a set of kinds of witchcraft, ranked by how deeply the practitioner is bound to demons, and calls for the worst of them to be burned or exterminated.
h: Those who conjure demons into a circle, glass, mirror, crystal, skull, ring or image make up the third kind of witch, deserving fire now and eternally ([p. 39](/book/699043bd288ef7d46205b914?page=39)).
The worst, fourth kind is women who have renounced baptism and given themselves by homage into the law and ownership of demons ([p. 39](/book/699043bd288ef7d46205b914?page=39)).
Trithemius says this fourth kind is to be utterly exterminated ([p. 39](/book/699043bd288ef7d46205b914?page=39)).

kb.t: Heinrich Cornelius Agrippa, Three Books of Occult Philosophy
kb.th: Agrippa presents magic as a learned art that works through the hidden virtues of things, numbers and words, linked by a graded sympathy that reaches up to celestial and divine powers.
h: Words and the names of things hold no less virtue than the affections of the mind, and composed speeches hold the most ([p. 109](/book/69bd9ca46120d54bd037001f?page=109)).

Mathematics is so necessary to magic that without it the magus labours in vain, since the lower world is made and governed by number, weight, measure, harmony, motion and light ([p. 217](/book/698420e1f1fb376a3d58061c?page=217)).

The planetary number tables have power only as signs of formal numbers ruled by divine intelligences, and each carries divine names, a good intelligence, an evil demon and a seal ([p. 292](/book/698420e1f1fb376a3d58061c?page=292)); ([p. 265](/book/69b642051c1c21a373889f10?page=265)).
Antipathy acts in sound as well as by contact, so a wolfskin drum silences one of sheepskin (p. 280).

Every person has three good guardian daemons, sacred, of the nativity and of the profession, and the sacred one is assigned by God, not by the stars ([p. 483](/book/698420e1f1fb376a3d58061c?page=483)).
tr: Agrippa's guardian daemon in III.22 is a good spirit, and rendering it in English as 'demon' turns a benevolent guardian into an evil one ([p. 483](/book/698420e1f1fb376a3d58061c?page=483)); (p. 333).
an: Papus (1893) moves the operative power from the graded sympathy Agrippa reports into the operator, defining magic as 'dynamized human will' applied to nature's living forces ([p. 382](/book/69bd9ca46120d54bd037001f?page=382)).

kb.t: Johann Reuchlin, On the Art of Kabbalah (De arte cabalistica)
kb.th: Reuchlin presents Kabbalah as a symbolic philosophy working through holy names toward salvation, and sets it against magic, which works through names of darkness toward perdition.
h: Kabbalah works through names of light and angels toward salvation, magic through names of darkness and evil spirits toward perdition ([p. 772](/book/69751588a88d83c830d99e18?page=772)).

Reuchlin calls Kabbalah 'a symbolic philosophy' and promises the Germans 'a Pythagoras reborn', claiming Pythagoras's philosophy began from the Cabalists' precepts ([p. 714](/book/6974b642457dd8909910b9e5?page=714)).
His Philolaus says Pythagoras received his doctrine from the Jews, should be called a Cabalist, and first renamed Cabala 'philosophy' ([p. 53](/book/69b51e359a81ef7feb3d1a02?page=53)).
tr: Reuchlin treats 'magician' as the accuser's label: Kabbalists' miracles came so easily that envious outsiders called them 'cunning magicians' ([p. 772](/book/69751588a88d83c830d99e18?page=772)).
For Reuchlin, magic names only the dark side of working with names, and Kabbalah names the holy side ([p. 772](/book/69751588a88d83c830d99e18?page=772)).

kb.t: Pietro Pomponazzi, On Incantations (De incantationibus)
kb.th: Pomponazzi argues that reported wonders and incantations can be explained by natural causes working through the heavens, without recourse to demons or angels, while some miracles exceed every natural cause.
h: Pomponazzi sets out to answer each reported wonder 'without recourse to demons or angels', placing the demon-based answer beside his own ([p. 165](/book/69905f2040bc3a0478efaf14?page=165)).
Plato posited demons only to instruct the common people, who picture them as bodily beings in a place ([p. 371](/book/69905f2040bc3a0478efaf14?page=371)).

For the Peripatetics wonders are worked by the intelligences through the celestial bodies, while for Christian doctrine angels or demons work them directly ([p. 371](/book/69905f2040bc3a0478efaf14?page=371)).

Whatever marvels demons can do, men can also do with no demon intervening, though Pomponazzi admits the hardest question is what directs a natural power to its target ([p. 247](/book/69905f2040bc3a0478efaf14?page=247)).

kb.t: Heinrich Cornelius Agrippa, On the Vanity of the Sciences (De vanitate)
kb.th: In De vanitate Agrippa separates natural magic, which brings nature's hidden powers into the open, from goetic sorcery worked through impure spirits, which he says all laws condemn.
h: Natural magic couples inferior things with superior gifts to bring nature's hidden powers into the open, the art acting as nature's minister ([p. 378](/book/69bd9ca46120d54bd037001f?page=378)).

Agrippa traces natural magic through Ethiopians, Indians, Brahmins, Gymnosophists, Egyptians and Persians, citing Cicero that no Persian took the kingdom without learning magic ([p. 378](/book/69bd9ca46120d54bd037001f?page=378)).
He says the Picatrix written for King Alfonso mixes much superstition with natural magic ([p. 99](/book/69520717ab34727b1f0436db?page=99)).
Goetic sorcery, worked through fellowship with impure spirits and forbidden conjurations, is by the consensus of all laws rooted out and cursed ([p. 205](/book/698420e1f1fb376a3d580616?page=205)).
Those who think they can constrain spirits by calling on the divine name are still in danger, even if they differ from those who worship devils ([p. 206](/book/698420e1f1fb376a3d580616?page=206)).
tr: Agrippa's 'magic' covers two opposed kinds: natural magic, which he defends, and goetia, which he names as the cursed art of impure spirits ([p. 378](/book/69bd9ca46120d54bd037001f?page=378)); ([p. 205](/book/698420e1f1fb376a3d580616?page=205)).
an: Papus (1893) relocates the power Agrippa's magi place in a graded sympathy into the operator's 'dynamized human will' ([p. 382](/book/69bd9ca46120d54bd037001f?page=382)).

it teacheth us by the agreement and the disagreement of things, either so to sunder them, or else to lay them so together by the mutual and fit applying of one thing to another, as thereby we do strange works, such as the vulgar sort call miracles

kb.t: Giambattista della Porta, Natural Magic (Magia naturalis)
kb.th: Porta takes magic to be the survey of the whole course of Nature: the practical part of natural philosophy, which works only through nature's own agreements and disagreements and has no place for the superstitious.
h: After reporting earlier definitions, Porta gives his own: magic is 'nothing else but the survey of the whole course of Nature' ([p. 16](/book/6953ea371479a63c11086267?page=16)); ([p. 17](/book/6953ea371479a63c11086267?page=17)).
Magic is nature's 'handmaid', and where natural affinity is too weak the art supplies the defect by timing and proportion, as husbandry does ([p. 16](/book/6953ea371479a63c11086267?page=16)).

Porta grounds the virtues of things in sympathy and antipathy, their hidden 'consent' and 'disagreement', and says the works the vulgar call miracles come from joining or sundering things by these ([p. 22](/book/6953ea371479a63c11086267?page=22)); ([p. 16](/book/6953ea371479a63c11086267?page=16)).

Porta places magic's flourishing in Ethiopia and India, which had great store of herbs and stones, and cites the Persian rule that no man might be king without learning magic ([p. 16](/book/6953ea371479a63c11086267?page=16)).

The 1560 Magia naturalis reports that Apulians bitten by the tarantula sing, weep, rave and dance, and are restored by melodies that soften the spirit ([p. 193](/book/695258d1ab34727b1f045aed?page=193)).
tr: Porta uses 'magic' approvingly, for a branch of natural philosophy that demands a perfect philosopher, and shuts the superstitious and wicked out of it, saying they deserve to be grievously punished ([p. 17](/book/6953ea371479a63c11086267?page=17)); ([p. 16](/book/6953ea371479a63c11086267?page=16)).
an: Goclenius builds his account of sympathy on iron and the magnet and cites Porta's term 'consensus' for it ([p. 22](/book/69907005245959b9547d626c?page=22)).
The Theatrum sympatheticum anthology prints Porta's chapter on sympathy and antipathy as its own chapter VII ([p. 38](/book/69b1d9bdbd74411f89f7233d?page=38)).

Tylor (1871) keeps Porta's link between magic and science but inverts its value, making occult science a mistaken inference from the association of ideas ([p. 16](/book/6953ea371479a63c11086267?page=16)).

Levinus Lemnius, The Secret Miracles of.a: Lemnius holds that Daemons, aerial Spirits who know things, mix with the humors, drive minds toward evil, and take part in storms, though winds could do the same damage alone. Good Spirits and angels assist the best things. He explains raving fever patients by disease and the humors, not a demon, and calls observing natural order lawful if not trusted too firmly.

q.t: Thus they [referring to the spirits] thrust themselves into storms, and sharpen the lightning and thunder, so much so that by their striving we see rooftops torn away, crops flattened, and cattle, herds, and flocks destroyed; although the violence and force of the winds might accomplish such a thing without them.

I have declared that such people are not tormented by an evil and hostile Spirit [original: Genio — a guiding or haunting spirit, here used in the context of potential possession.], nor do they perform these things by the instinct and impulse of a demon, but rather by the power of the disease and the ferocity of the humors; by these, as if a torch were applied, the mind of man blazes up and is inflamed.

Furthermore, it is lawful to examine and observe those things that consist in the natural order of things, and no law forbids it; provided, however, that we do not rely upon them too rigidly or firmly, since conjectures very often do not lead to the desired outcome.

kb.t: Pseudo-Agrippa, Fourth Book of Occult Philosophy
kb.th: The Fourth Book presents itself as the practical key to Agrippa's three books of occult philosophy, supplying the names, circles, perfumes and rites for calling spirits and the dead.
h: It calls itself a 'Complement and Key' to the books of Occult Philosophy and to all magical operations, and asks the reader to keep it secret ([p. 51](/book/695234e3ab34727b1f044dc2?page=51)).

It derives the names of the planetary intelligences, and of the princes of evil spirits, by collecting letters out of an astrological figure of the world ([p. 51](/book/695234e3ab34727b1f044dc2?page=51)).
The circle is fortified with divine names and the names of good spirits able to bind the spirit called ([p. 83](/book/695234e3ab34727b1f044dc2?page=83)).

Lights, perfumes and unguents work for two reasons, by natural and celestial agreement with the spirit and as worship offered to it, which the text itself calls 'superstitious' ([p. 83](/book/695234e3ab34727b1f044dc2?page=83)).

Souls of the dead are not called up without blood or part of the body, and places of execution and recent slaughter rank above churchyards for raising them ([p. 87](/book/695234e3ab34727b1f044dc2?page=87)).
an: Johann Weyer, Agrippa's pupil, rejected it as an 'abominable little book' attributed to Agrippa by a wicked man ([p. 163](/book/695925acaecc3a7338f964dc?page=163)).

kb.t: Johann Weyer, On the Tricks of Demons (De praestigiis daemonum)
kb.th: Weyer, a physician, argues that the witches of the trials are deluded women whose imaginations are corrupted by melancholy, and keeps his severity for learned ritual magicians.
h: Weyer says he wrote because he saw the confessions of insane old women taken as truth, with no line drawn between deluded witches and actual poisoners ([p. 28](/book/695925a9aecc3a7338f962f1?page=28)).
He explains the witches' experiences by a corrupted imagination, as in melancholics whose humor occupies the brain ([p. 193](/book/695925a9aecc3a7338f962f1?page=193)).
For a repentant deluded witch he proposes at most a fine, a non-capital punishment or temporary exile ([p. 475](/book/695925a9aecc3a7338f962f1?page=475)).
He complains that learned 'sacrilegious magicians', punished severely under the Old Law, now live with impunity and even praise ([p. 28](/book/695925a9aecc3a7338f962f1?page=28)).

He rejects the Fourth Book as an 'abominable little book' falsely given to Agrippa, and judges books ascribed to Raziel and Raphael to be recent forgeries ([p. 163](/book/695925acaecc3a7338f964dc?page=163)).
tr: The title's word praestigium, as Isidore derives it, comes from 'blinding the sight of the eyes' and names illusion, with no power over things ([p. 331](/book/69af2339285bd73604373fd4?page=331)).
an: Jean Bodin quotes Weyer's definition of the witch as acting from an imaginary pact and glosses it as someone thought to do with demons' help what she does not actually do ([p. 493](/book/695925eb15b4070cb1e7fe1f?page=493)).

Bodin attacks Weyer for appending to the 1578 edition an index of the 'diabolical monarchy' naming 72 princes and 7,405,926 devils, with their uses for invocation ([p. 462](/book/69905e022fd6a039938a0803?page=462)).

kb.t: John Dee, The Hieroglyphic Monad (Monas hieroglyphica)
kb.th: Dee presents his monad as a 'MAGIC Parable': a single sign, explained mathematically, magically, cabalistically and anagogically, from which the order of created things can be read.

The work announces that it is explained 'mathematically, magically, cabalistically, and anagogically' ([p. 23](/book/6952d04f77f38f6761bc4ee2?page=23)).

It opens with a Euclidean theorem: by the straight line and the circle the first representation of things hidden in nature was brought to light, and by the point and the monad things first began to exist ([p. 23](/book/6952d04f77f38f6761bc4ee2?page=23)).

kb.t: Arbatel: On the Magic of the Ancients (Arbatel de magia veterum)
kb.th: The Arbatel presents a Christian magic of the ancients, in which the true Magus is served by God for knowledge of creation and is set against the sorcerer served by evil spirits.
h: The 1686 German version titles itself the magic and wisdom of the people of God and of the heathen Magi, written 'against the devil-sorcerers', in aphorisms taught 'by the spirits' ([p. 7](/book/6981920786654d9d793ff3a2?page=7)).

It defines the Magus as one whom the Divine Essence serves for knowledge of creation, and the Cacomagus as one whom evil spirits serve, by God's permission, to ruin ([p. 33](/book/6981920786654d9d793ff3a2?page=33)).
Its Olympic spirit Och administers solar matters, extends life to 600 years, teaches medicine and turns everything into gold and precious stones ([p. 17](/book/6981920786654d9d793ff3a2?page=17)).
The first of its seven greatest secrets is to heal all diseases within seven days by characters, natural means or the higher stars, with God's help ([p. 22](/book/6981920786654d9d793ff3a2?page=22)).
tr: The Arbatel keeps 'Magus' as an honourable name for one God serves and gives the hostile practitioner a separate name, Cacomagus, rendered in German as 'Devil-Sorcerer', so that magic itself stays on the lawful side of the line ([p. 33](/book/6981920786654d9d793ff3a2?page=33)); ([p. 7](/book/6981920786654d9d793ff3a2?page=7)).

kb.t: Jean Bodin, On the Demon-Mania of Witches (De la démonomanie des sorciers)
kb.th: Bodin writes a handbook for judges that defines the sorcerer as one who knowingly seeks an end by diabolical means, making intent part of the crime.
h: Bodin defines the sorcerer as one who knowingly strives to achieve something by diabolical means, and says earlier writers gave no definition ([p. 37](/book/695925eb15b4070cb1e7fe1f?page=37)).
A sick person who uses a diabolical remedy in good faith, from a sorcerer taken for an honest man, is in his view no sorcerer ([p. 37](/book/695925eb15b4070cb1e7fe1f?page=37)).
He closes by refuting Weyer, turning Weyer's definition of the witch as acting from an imaginary pact against him ([p. 493](/book/695925eb15b4070cb1e7fe1f?page=493)).
He attacks Weyer for printing an index of 72 princes and 7,405,926 devils with their uses for invocation ([p. 462](/book/69905e022fd6a039938a0803?page=462)).
tr: The 1581 Latin version renders Bodin's sorcier with magus, so the learned Latin word carries the French accuser's sense of one who knowingly uses diabolical means ([p. 35](/book/69905e022fd6a039938a0803?page=35)).
Bodin's definition leaves no room for a lawful magus: in his usage the word names a crime ([p. 37](/book/695925eb15b4070cb1e7fe1f?page=37)); ([p. 35](/book/69905e022fd6a039938a0803?page=35)).
an: Against Bodin's individual definition, Thomasius (1701) tested the alleged personal pact, and Doutté (1909), following Hubert and Mauss, made magic a collective creation answering collective needs ([p. 37](/book/695925eb15b4070cb1e7fe1f?page=37)).

kb.t: Reginald Scot, The Discoverie of Witchcraft
kb.th: Scot argues that witchcraft is a matter of poor, deluded women, a feared name and conjurers' tricks, and that no witch or devil can command nature.
h: Those called witches are, in one sort, poor, old, infirm and superstitious women easily persuaded that misfortunes around them are their own doing ([p. 101](/book/695926cc15b4070cb1e80050?page=101)).
The name of witch is so odious and feared that even the most honest person arraigned on it will hardly escape condemnation ([p. 101](/book/695926cc15b4070cb1e80050?page=101)).

James VI of Scotland, Daemonologie|||Dem.a: In James's dialogue, Epistemon divides the devil's art into two kinds, Magic or Necromancy and Sorcery or Witchcraft. The devil's "rudiments" are the power of word, herb and stone, meaning charms and superstitions that lack natural causes. Epistemon says the sin against the Holy Ghost has two branches, and necromancers, enchanters and witches fall under the first. He cites the Law of God as prohibiting and threatening magicians, diviners, enchanters, sorcerers and witches. He treats Pharaoh's wise men, the Pythoness Saul consulted, Simon Magus and the Python-spirit woman of Acts 16 as practitioners, and he answers a medical argument from melancholy.

kb.t: Francis Bacon, The Advancement of Learning (De augmentis scientiarum)

He separates 'Celestiall Magique', the capture of a favourable star aspect in seals and rings, from sound astrology and calls it 'Astrologicall Frenzie' ([p. 273](/book/6953e50b77f38f6761befa1e?page=273)).

J. B. van Helmont, On the Magnetic Cure.a: Van Helmont holds that the Soul has a Magical Virtue infused by its Creator, able to act per nutum, by intuition, at a distance. He says Natural Magick rests on this virtue and in no respect on benedictions, ceremonies and superstitions. The magician always uses a medium, and an object that is disposed or weak and conscious of guilt, such as the witch, surrenders to the Magnetism. Exorcisms fail when the exorcist's mind is dully excited. He ascribes the unguent's cure to the Magnet and an Ecstatick power in the blood, and denies it comes from Satan.

q.t: The mark we shot at was, that there is inhabitant in the Soul a certain Magical Virtue, infused by the primitive bounty of her Creator, naturally proper and of right belonging to her by that just title, that Man is the image and noble effigies of the Deity;

I say, the magician ever makes use of a medium: for thus, unless a pregnant woman hath extended her hand to her own thigh, forehead, or buttocks, the infant in her womb shall never be stigmatized in his thigh, forehead, or buttocks.

Lo now you have the true and positive reason of the Natural Magnetism in the Unguent, deduced from Natural Magick; to which the Soul of Reason, and Light of Truth is pleased to assent, in that sentence, Where the treasure is, there the heart is also:

Pierre de Lancre, Incredulity and Misbel.a: De Lancre says nothing alleged of sorcerers is impossible to the Demon, and that examples and the accused's own confessions confirm it. He treats the words magician and sorcerer as interchangeable, all enrolled under Satan's banner, and cites a pact written on a two of hearts. He argues that a brass serpent hidden under a Lausanne threshold afflicted a whole family and its animals, which imagination alone could not do, since imagination is not hereditary.

q.t: For the response is, that there is nothing of all this impossible to the Demon, and that every thing of which they are accused is found confirmed by so many notable examples, indeed by their own confessions, that there is no man, however learned or ignorant he may be, who can contradict or deny them.
And since there are Demons, there is also a certain Demonic Magic practiced by Magicians and Sorcerers; for these words are used interchangeably today.

And in the Diocese of Lausanne, a Sorceress having hidden a brass serpent under the threshold of a door, rendered a whole family impotent, so much so that not even the animals nor the beasts of burden could conceive or bring their young to perfection.

He argues that magicians' wonders differ from the miracles of Moses and Christ, and that images and characters cannot draw celestial influences.

kb.t: Gabriel Naudé, Apology for Great Men Accused of Magic
kb.th: Naudé defends learned men accused of magic by testing the stories told against them, and he faults the demonologists for believing every tale.
h: Naudé finds it 'a strange thing' that Delrio, Le Loyer, Bodin, de Lancre and Godelmann never rejected any story, 'though ever so fabulous' ([p. 328](/book/699201577c226bdd25f98855?page=328)).

He reports the legend that Albertus Magnus cast a metal 'Androides' under the constellations, which answered questions until Aquinas smashed it, and traces the fable to the Hebrew teraph ([p. 269](/book/69c879e06c6f3cc53c858579?page=269)).
He agrees with Trithemius in mocking the works attributed to Albert the Great as spurious ([p. 101](/book/6974b63b19126e775cf6d7cb?page=101)).
tr: Naudé sorts magic by its agent into four kinds, Divine, Theurgic, Goetic and Natural, keeping the word 'magic' for all four and confining the demonic to the Goetic alone ([p. 34](/book/69c879e06c6f3cc53c858579?page=34)).

He reads Pliny's list of philosopher-travellers as an attempt 'to soil them with the stains of Magic', treating 'magus' as an accuser's label for Pythagoras, Empedocles, Democritus and Plato ([p. 311](/book/699201597c226bdd25f989ad?page=311)).

kb.t: Francis Bacon, Sylva Sylvarum
kb.th: In the Sylva Sylvarum Bacon treats the weapon-salve as a reported marvel to be recorded with caution, and he is sceptical of the excuses magical medicine makes when it fails.

Jacques Gaffarel, Unheard-of Curiosities.a: Gaffarel supports the efficacy of talismanic figures with three arguments: the influence of the stars, the power of sympathy, and experience. kb.t: William Foster, Hoplocrisma-spongus: a Sponge to Wipe Away the Weapon-Salve
kb.th: Foster attacks the weapon-salve as a magical cure that the Church condemns, and he denies that any sympathy joins the wound and the weapon.

an: Robert Fludd replied, stating Foster's question as whether weapon-salve healing is sorcery and denying that it is ([p. 6](/book/6988a5a1fc4961cb1cc53ea8?page=6)).

kb.t: The Lesser Key of Solomon: Goetia
kb.th: The Goetia is a working catalogue of seventy-two spirits once sealed by Solomon, with the seals, circle, triangle and formulas by which an operator calls, commands and dismisses them.

The seals of the spirits are to be made in the metal of the planet matching each rank: kings in gold, marquises in silver, dukes in copper, and so on ([p. 59](/book/695285d5ab34727b1f04c36f?page=59)).
The first spirit, Bael, makes one go invisible, and his character must be worn as a lamen by the caller, 'or else he will not do thee homage' ([p. 35](/book/695285d5ab34727b1f04c36f?page=35)).

The circle of Solomon is nine feet across and ringed with divine names from Ehyeh to Levanah, with the triangle into which spirits are commanded standing two feet outside it ([p. 62](/book/695285d5ab34727b1f04c36f?page=62)).
An operation ends with a formal 'license to the spirit that he may depart', sending it back to its dwelling without terror to men or any creature ([p. 93](/book/695285d5ab34727b1f04c36f?page=93)).

He invokes Roger Bacon's De nullitate magiae, with Dee's notes, in support ([p. 287](/book/69906181322e01b1349a4aa9?page=287)).

Dee, whose notes Webster cites, defines Thaumaturgike as the mathematical art of making strange works that are greatly wondered at, such as the pneumatic devices of Ctesibius and Hero ([p. 55](/book/69aebe88a103e42dc94145ad?page=55)).

q.t: there is a latent Atheism at the root of the Saducean Principle. For too many deny Witches, because they believe there are no Spirits, and they are so persuaded, because they own no being in the World but Matter, and the results of Motion
And we know not but the Laws of that dark kingdom may enjoyn a particular attendance upon all those that practise their Mysteries, whether they know them to be theirs, or not.

The witch provides the occasion, but is not the primary cause [original: "Principal Efficient"]. She appears to perform the act, but the spirit carries out the wonder—sometimes directly, as in physical transportations and possessions; sometimes by using other natural causes, as in raising storms and inflicting diseases; and sometimes using the witch as a tool [original: "Instrument"], conveying harmful influences through the eyes or touch.

kb.t: Joseph Glanvill, Saducismus triumphatus
kb.th: Glanvill defends the reality of witches and spirits and treats their denial as a hidden atheism that admits nothing beyond matter and motion.
h: Glanvill argues there is 'a latent Atheism' in disbelief of witches ([p. 461](/book/6952db2477f38f6761bc70c4?page=461)).
In his account people deny witches because they deny spirits, and deny spirits because they own nothing but matter and motion ([p. 461](/book/6952db2477f38f6761bc70c4?page=461)).
On the Tedworth disturbances he witnessed, he concludes there was 'somewhat extraordinary, and what we usually call preternatural in the business' ([p. 286](/book/6952db2477f38f6761bc70c4?page=286)).
tr: Glanvill uses the English 'preternatural' as the ordinary word for a poltergeist's doings, and the word is reported to have run at the same time in a medical sense for diseases 'praeter naturam' ([p. 286](/book/6952db2477f38f6761bc70c4?page=286)); (p. 34).

kb.t: Balthasar Bekker, The World Bewitched (De betoverde weereld)
kb.th: Bekker, a Cartesian minister, argues that a bodiless devil can do nothing above nature, so sorcery by pact cannot exist.
h: Bekker concludes that sorcery as commonly understood, effects beyond nature worked by the devil's power through a pact, cannot exist ([p. 670](/book/69b176971643b0f241bd0349?page=670)).
He reasons that the devil can do nothing above nature and, lacking a body, can do less upon bodies than a human can ([p. 670](/book/69b176971643b0f241bd0349?page=670)).

He reads Psalm 96:5 as calling the gods of the peoples 'Nothings', and holds that Scripture names Daimones only to signify what exists in heathen imagination ([p. 557](/book/69b176971643b0f241bd0349?page=557)).

His conclusion marks the far end of a shift from Del Rio, for whom magic was an art working wonders 'by a created and non-supernatural power', to magic as error ([p. 31](/book/698fb9446b95eeda7d2d38b9?page=31)).

Cotton Mather, The Wonders of the Invisi.a: Mather names "lesser sorceries" said to be common in New England, such as curing injuries with spells and conjurations with sieves, keys, peas, nails and horseshoes. He holds that these practices lead people into witchcraft and that a devil may become a familiar spirit to the practitioner. He quotes Perkins and Gaule on signs for detecting witches, including a compact, and describes devils as organised under a prince.

q.t: It is in the Devil's name that such things are done; and in God's name, I do this day charge them as vile acts of ungodliness.
Now, some devil is always invited into the service of the person who practices these witchcrafts.

To worship the Devil is witchcraft, and under that notion our Lord was urged to sin. We are told in 1 Samuel 15:23, Rebellion is as the sin of witchcraft. When the Devil would have us sin, he would have us do the things which the wretched witches usually do.

Every crime consists of a fact. A fact is not presumed. Therefore, he who asserts that the crime of Magic exists must prove it, rather than demanding proof from the one who denies it.

he was so far from explicitly arranging anything in that Constitution … regarding Magic that involves a pact with the Devil … inflicts harm or disadvantage upon people through sorcery, they shall be punished from life to death, and such punishment shall be carried out with fire.

kb.t: Christian Thomasius, On the Crime of Magic (De crimine magiae)
kb.th: Thomasius, a jurist, tests the crime of magic itself, setting out the alleged pact with the devil and holding that whoever says the crime exists must prove it.
h: Thomasius sets out the alleged pact: the devil satisfies a person's lust, greed or ambition in return for fornication, flight, worship and dancing, harm by storms to people, beasts and crops, and eternal servitude ([p. 14](/book/699043ba288ef7d46205b8a3?page=14)).
He argues that a crime consists of a fact, a fact is not presumed, and so whoever asserts the crime of magic exists must prove it ([p. 14](/book/699043ba288ef7d46205b8a3?page=14)).

He reads Carolina art. 109 as saying nothing about a pact: it punishes harmful sorcery with fire and leaves harmless sorcery to discretionary punishment ([p. 31](/book/699043ba288ef7d46205b8a3?page=31)).

The pact he tests is a personal one, the individual frame that Doutté (1909), following Hubert and Mauss, replaced with magic as 'originally a collective creation' ([p. 37](/book/695925eb15b4070cb1e7fe1f?page=37)).
tr: In the German law Thomasius reads, sorcery is the name of a crime, and the statute grades it by harm done with no mention of a pact ([p. 31](/book/699043ba288ef7d46205b8a3?page=31)).

q.t: And grant him favor, grace, and mercy before the Throne of the Lord and before all creatures who see him.

The names emerging from this verse are very good for protection, so that no sorcery may cause harm. "Behold" [original: Hineh] has the numerical value of "Vessel" [original: Keli]; this is a name from the 72-letter Name to break every sorcery, for no sorcery can pass through except by way of a "vessel."

Another for love: Write with rose water and saffron [Saffron was a highly valued and "solar" ingredient in medieval magic] using a copper pen on kosher parchment in the name of [Person A, son of Mother] so that the heart of [Person B, son/daughter of Mother] shall be bound to the love of [Person A] to do his will and desire.

kb.t: Sefer Raziel ha-Malakh (The Book of the Angel Raziel), Hebrew
kb.th: Sefer Raziel treats the written names of angels as protective and effective powers, set down on amulets that guard mother and child and win the bearer favor.
h: A childbirth amulet adjures 'First Eve', Lilith, by the three angels Senoi, Sansenoi and Semangelof not to harm mother or child ([p. 106](/book/6985ca7194b042cd03912166?page=106)).
Other amulets serve social ends, such as gaining favor and grace before all who see the bearer ([p. 104](/book/6985ca7194b042cd03912166?page=104)).
an: Maimonides objects to this kind of practical name-magic: he holds that the invented names of amulet writers have no power and that a perfect man should not even listen to them ([p. 180](/book/697a8670e680cef7cedae3aa?page=180)).
A 1635 Latin cabalistic disputation explains why Jews hang a kamea with the three angels' names on infants: Lilith swore not to harm where she saw their names (p. 390).

Montgomery's edition of the Nippur incantation bowls traces angel names on the bowls to the Book of Raziel, linking late-antique Babylonian Jewish magic with the later Raziel literature ([p. 159](/book/6953af0577f38f6761bd92a5?page=159)).

Le Petit Albert (Secrets of Natural and.a: The chapter on talismans traces their antiquity and uses. It names the Egyptian images of Isis, Serapis and Osiris, the Hebrew characters, and the pentacle with angel names on one side and God's names on the other. It also describes the Paracelsus medal with the brazen serpent of Moses, and the celandine gathered at full or new moon, as preservatives against plague. Other chapters treat physiognomy and chiromancy, which the book defines as divination by the look of the hand.

q.t: The name Talisman has been given to all medals or carved pieces, of skin and parchment, upon which are imaged Hebrew characters, supposedly having marvelous virtues, or else they are representations of planets or zodiacal signs, which are classified in the science called astrology.

The principal talismans are often represented by astrological images, that is to say, by figures of planets or constellations, which have the goal of preserving from shipwrecks, diseases, storms, or violent death; sometimes they are mixed with profane names, the names of God, of our divine savior, and of good angels.

The rabbis, who made a profession of occult philosophy, affected in their theology and mysteries of their religion to employ sacred words to make the oracles speak and thus acted in their practices of enchantments, spells, and divinations.

Francis Hutchinson, An Historical Essay.a: Hutchinson examines the words sorcery, witch, enchanter and conjurer and how translators have rendered the Hebrew terms in Deuteronomy 18. He sets out the kinds of witch named in the books, including the witch by art and the witch by compact. He ties the biblical texts on witchcraft to idolatry and to Simon Magus, discusses King James's Daemonologie and the 1604 statute, and lists trial practices such as swimming and the search for teats.

q.t: Our law [original: "Statute"] forbids every kind of use and exercise of any sorcery or charm for employing spirits. It punishes the guilty person with death if they do harm to man or beast, and with imprisonment and the pillory [term: a wooden frame with holes for the head and hands, used for public punishment and humiliation] even if their charms have no effect.

Sorcery is one of the most common names in our law books for witchcraft and is classified as a felony by our statutes. But those who would try to define the crime based on its name would be wasting their time; for strictly speaking, sorcery means nothing more than drawing lots [original: "Lottery"; derived from the Old French sorcerie, related to sors (lot or fate).]

For there is, as the books on this subject tell us, the "cursing witch" and the "blessing witch"; the witch by art [original: "Witch by Art" — Someone who uses learned rituals, spells, or alchemy to perform magic.] and the witch by compact [original: "Compact" — A formal agreement or contract, typically a soul-selling deal with the Devil.].

Book of segulot (Sifre madaʿ segulot, Ga.a: The manuscript gives a remedy of salt in water placed outside the house, said to send away the mazikin, fever and illness. Its childbirth section offers methods against the demon and Lilith, including the sign Tayam (444, the gematria of Chiran). Other entries annul water sorcery with divine names, give a charm called Leaping of the Way, and write names against fever. Pages on food and the Sabbath tie the meal to the sefirot and to focus on the Tetragrammaton.

Eberhard David Hauber, Bibliotheca acta.a: Hauber's pages define forbidden magic as diabolical Zauberey, a crime founded on a pact with the Devil, with sensual pleasure, flight through the air, worship, dancing and harm to people as its described results. One argument holds that people can reach pleasure, honor and wealth without the Devil. It adds that the Devil gains nothing from a pact, since those given to vice already belong to him. Another writer sorts effects into purely natural, mixed, and wholly Satan's, and lists the means of harm: words, written notes, seals, wax images, amulets, characters and items made from human hair or fat.

q.t: Here, however, we are speaking only of forbidden magic—namely, diabolical magic, which in our mother tongue is usually called witchcraft [original: "Zauberey"].

Humans can achieve all those things which are stated as the purposes of a pact with the Devil—sensual pleasure, honor, and wealth—without the Devil’s help. Why then should they make a pact with the Devil?

He writes that some effects of the same occur purely naturally, as do lice, mice, fleas, etc.; others are mixed with natural and devilish things, such as weather-making, blinding, Beschreyen bewitching by praise/glamour, etc.; but some depend entirely on Satan, to which nature contributes nothing, such as flying to the Blocks-Berge Brocken Mountain (a legendary site of witches' gatherings).

Augustin Calmet, Dissertations on Appari.a: Calmet says the law of God, Moses, the Church, and secular judges punish the impiety and superstition of those who consult or trust the demon, and he adds that imaginary invalids are cured, not executed. He names Pharaoh's magicians, Simon the Magician, Bar-Jesus, and the Pythoness as real cases. In his letter on another author's book, he argues that if sorcery and magic both work wonders through the demon, their essence is the same, and that tacit pacts would make the devil a kind of God.

q.t: Now, it is the folly, the vain credulity, and the prejudice of these sorts of people that the law of God forbids, that Moses condemns to death, that the Christian Church punishes by its censures, and that secular judges repress with the utmost rigor.

In treating sorcery and magic in this book, it is asserted that the demon intervenes in both, and that both perform wonders. But if that is the case, it is impossible to find any difference between them.

Do we not see that this opinion leads to making the devil a God? For if someone, for example, living two or three hundred leagues from us, has made a pact with the demon, that whenever a pendulum is suspended over a glass, it will mark the hour as regularly as the most exact clock;

David Hume, Of Miracles (An Enquiry conc.a: Hume defines a miracle in a footnote as a transgression of a law of nature by a particular volition of the Deity or an invisible agent. He sets a maxim that testimony suffices only if its falsehood would be more miraculous than the fact, and he weighs one miracle against the other. He quotes Bacon that accounts depending on religion, and the writers of natural magic or alchemy, are suspicious.

q.t: A miracle may be accurately defined as a transgression of a law of nature by a particular volition of the Deity, or by the interposition of some invisible agent.

Above all, every account must be considered as suspicious that depends in any degree upon religion, such as the prodigies of Livy [Roman historian known for recording numerous omens and portents.]. And no less so, everything found in the writers of natural magic or alchemy, or such authors.

kb.t: Grimorium verum
kb.th: The Grimorium Verum treats magic as dealing with demons by pact, aided by the sympathy between certain stones and the spirits.
h: The Grimorium Verum says there are only two kinds of pact, tacit and explicit ([p. 4](/book/695936603b43cb6630c9171f?page=4)).
It warns the operator to beware spirits that require something belonging to him ([p. 4](/book/695936603b43cb6630c9171f?page=4)).
It lets a spirit's character be drawn on an emerald or ruby, 'for they have a sympathy for the spirits, especially those of the Sun' ([p. 4](/book/695936603b43cb6630c9171f?page=4)).
The character is to be written in the operator's own blood ([p. 4](/book/695936603b43cb6630c9171f?page=4)).
an: Waite (1898) judged the work's printed date 'undeniably fraudulent' and placed it in the mid-eighteenth century ([p. 103](/book/69c896426c6f3cc53c85c4ea?page=103)).

Waite repeats its division of pacts into tacit and manifest, and, citing Bergier's Theological Dictionary, notes that Catholic theologians extended the pact to cover the mere act of communicating with spirits ([p. 259](/book/69c896426c6f3cc53c85c4ea?page=259)).

kb.t: Le Grand Grimoire (Le Dragon rouge)
kb.th: The Grand Grimoire treats magic as a written bargain with a demon, exchanging a later reward for treasure now.
h: The Grand Grimoire gives a pact with Lucifuge Rofocale, written by hand on virgin parchment ([p. 68](/book/695929fe7c072c27f686d4bd?page=68)).
The pact is signed in the operator's own blood ([p. 68](/book/695929fe7c072c27f686d4bd?page=68)).
In return for treasures given, the signer promises to reward Lucifuge in twenty years ([p. 68](/book/695929fe7c072c27f686d4bd?page=68)).
an: Waite (1898) dated the Grand Grimoire no earlier than the mid-eighteenth century, the date he gave the Grimorium Verum ([p. 103](/book/69c896426c6f3cc53c85c4ea?page=103)).

kb.t: Pseudo-Faust, Natural and Unnatural Magic, or the Triple Coercion of Hell
kb.th: This Faust text treats magic as the coercion of hell's spirits, ranked by how useful they are for finding treasure and minerals.
h: Scheible's 1849 Stuttgart edition prints the text from a decorated manuscript in the Ducal Library at Coburg ([p. 5](/book/69592a007c072c27f686d518?page=5)).
Speaking in Faust's voice, the text ranks the spirits of hell by usefulness ([p. 13](/book/69592a007c072c27f686d518?page=13)).
It claims that without the spirit Marbuel 'no secret can be discovered regarding minerals' and hidden riches ([p. 13](/book/69592a007c072c27f686d518?page=13)).
It conjures Mephistophiel by a string of names to appear before the circle and answer 'in the German language' ([p. 69](/book/69592a007c072c27f686d518?page=69)).

Yi Man-un, Kinyŏn aram|||Korean & Vietna.a: Yi Man-un's text is a chronological list of state events, and the witchcraft cases appear as short entries among them. The Sin-sa entry says that after Queen Inhyeon died a witchcraft plot was found, and court ladies, shamans, Jang Hui-jae, and Min Eon-nyang were executed. An earlier entry for 1532 records witchcraft in the palace in which Royal Consort Gyeong, her son Prince Bokseong, and Hong Ryeo were killed and later exonerated.

q.t: The Sin-sa Witchcraft Trial. After Queen Inhyeon passed away, a plot involving witchcraft was discovered. Court ladies, shamans, Jang Hui-jae, and Min Eon-nyang were executed.
A case of witchcraft occurred in the palace. Royal Consort Gyeong of the Park clan, her son Prince Bokseong, and the Royal Son-in-law Hong Ryeo were all tragically killed. They were later exonerated.

3rd. This reciprocal action is subject to mechanical laws, which have remained unknown until the present time.
It is through this operation—the most universal of all those offered to us by Nature—that the active relationships are exercised between the celestial bodies, the earth, and its constituent parts.

kb.t: Franz Anton Mesmer, Mémoire sur la découverte du magnétisme animal
kb.th: Mesmer presents animal magnetism as physics: a universal fluid, obeying mechanical laws, links the stars, the earth and living bodies.
h: Mesmer's first two propositions posit a mutual influence between celestial bodies, the earth and living bodies, carried by a universally distributed fluid that leaves no vacuum ([p. 86](/book/6990580e1729589044135366?page=86)).
His third proposition holds that this action obeys mechanical laws hitherto unknown ([p. 86](/book/6990580e1729589044135366?page=86)).
He describes the fluid's action as an alternating 'ebb and flow', which he calls the most universal operation of Nature ([p. 87](/book/6990580e1729589044135366?page=87)).

A later section bound in the same volume is reported to liken staged convulsive cures to St. Médard and Loudun as 'the basis of all impostures', and to class Gassner's cures with them ([p. 304](/book/6990580e1729589044135366?page=304)).
an: Puységur reduces the whole doctrine to the operator's belief in a power within and the will to use it, 'croyez et veuillez' (p. 157).

Lévi calls Mesmer's tub 'a rather imperfect magic chain' and recasts collective enthusiasm as a magnetic current ([p. 188](/book/6a21981d5ce215cb9ac711d9?page=188)); ([p. 255](/book/6a21981d5ce215cb9ac711d9?page=255)).
Eddy calls animal magnetism 'the human antipode of divine Science' and cites the 1784 commissioners' finding that there is no magnetic fluid ([p. 504](/book/6a5837d96701425b993051ba?page=504)).

q.t: Magnetism is therefore nothing but an old error. This theory is presented today with a more imposing apparatus—necessary in a more enlightened age—but it is nonetheless false. Man grasps, abandons, and then retakes the error that flatters him.

kb.t: Nicolas Bergasse, Considérations sur le magnétisme animal
kb.th: Bergasse, Mesmer's leading disciple, argues that universal magnetism can be shown experimentally only through its effects on sick bodies.
h: Bergasse argues that universal magnetism produces sensation only in a sick organised body ([p. 115](/book/6991bd4570254d38471e3940?page=115)).
He concludes that only the sick can serve as experimental proof that the magnetism exists ([p. 115](/book/6991bd4570254d38471e3940?page=115)).
an: Puységur reports that his patient Victor, put into the 'magnetic state', prescribed his own bleeding, an idea that terrified him once he returned to his natural state ([p. 233](/book/69905f1440bc3a0478efa351?page=233)).

However, along with man, magic also degenerated. When men have great knowledge and no good heart, they soon apply their science to evil. So it went there too, and there arose magia veneficia poisonous or sorcerous magic, necromantia necromancy; communication with the dead, black magic.

The second makes a pansophist a man who has mastery over all sciences that constitute erudition. Finally, the third and last degree makes a magus a wise man who applies and uses all this knowledge according to the plan of the Deity for the benefit of mankind.

kb.t: Karl von Eckartshausen, Disclosures on Magic (Aufschlüsse zur Magie)
kb.th: Eckartshausen holds that true magic is the highest science of the relationships of natural things, set within a Christian theosophy, while treating stage conjuring as deception through speed.
h: Eckartshausen defines true magic as the highest perfection of natural and creaturely wisdom and the highest science of the relationships of natural things ([p. 417](/book/69c844a66c6f3cc53c85135b?page=417)).
He places this definition after a passage on the Christian's transformed heart ([p. 417](/book/69c844a66c6f3cc53c85135b?page=417)).

The book ends with numbered conjuring recipes and a 'theory of speed and the art of sleight of hand', holding that there are 'thousands of kinds of natural magic tricks' ([p. 500](/book/69c844a66c6f3cc53c85135b?page=500)).
Eckartshausen explains prestidigitation as deception through speed ([p. 500](/book/69c844a66c6f3cc53c85135b?page=500)).
tr: The book uses the word magic in two senses: 'true magic' is the highest science of natural relationships, and 'natural magic tricks' is the conjurer's repertoire of sleight of hand ([p. 417](/book/69c844a66c6f3cc53c85135b?page=417)).

Romanusbüchlein|||Grimoires.a: The book gives short charms, each ending with the Trinity or the letters J. J. J. For a cow whose milk has been taken, the text says a Nimmfrau has been there. For wounds, it directs that the four rivers of Paradise be written on paper and laid on the wound. It also gives a thief-binding that invokes the three nails of Christ, greased with Armensünder-Schmalz, and a Sator Square for livestock against witchcraft and the work of the devil.
