q.t: The Hindoo "adept" becomes able, through a certain training of mind, to send his spirit or himself from his body. It is still connected with it by the fine unseen current of life known in the Bible as the "silver thread."
But no one can be a true Occultist without being a real Theosophist; otherwise he is simply a black magician, whether conscious or unconscious.

Magic is the science of communicating with and directing supernal supramundane powers, as well as commanding those of lower spheres; it is a practical knowledge of the hidden mysteries of nature which are known only to the few, because they are so difficult to acquire without falling into sin against the law. Ancient and medieval mystics divided magic into three classes—Theurgia, Goetia, and Natural Magic.

They should instead address their Higher Spiritual Ego, which is bathed in the light of the Spirit-Soul [original: Atma-Buddhic], and say, "Thy will be done, not mine," and so on. To use this power for selfish ends is black magic, an abomination, and spiritual sorcery.

kb.t: H. P. Blavatsky, The Key to Theosophy
kb.th: The Key to Theosophy binds occult practice to Theosophy itself: whoever takes up occultism without being a true Theosophist is counted a black magician.
h: An Occultist who is not a real Theosophist is 'simply a black magician, whether conscious or unconscious' ([p. 43](/book/69528a11ab34727b1f04e1cb?page=43)).
Blavatsky had earlier set out, in Isis Unveiled, that arcane knowledge misapplied is sorcery and beneficently used is true magic or wisdom ([p. 603](/book/6953e33477f38f6761bebf10?page=603)).

q.t: You shall keep them to hang from your neck—whichever one you wish—on the day and hour in which you were born. After this, you shall take care to speak the Name that is hung from your neck ten times every day while turning toward the East; you may be certain that no enchantment or any other danger shall have the power to harm you.

There are also spirits in the Elements as well as in the Heavens: some in the Region of Fire, others in the Air, others in the Water, and others upon the Earth. All of these can serve the man who learns their nature and knows how to attract them.

After this he will see the Spirits come from every side. But in case they are occupied in some other place, or that they cannot come, or that they are unwilling to come: then let him begin again to invoke them in the following manner, and let the Exorcist be assured that even if they were bound with chains of iron and with fire, they could not refrain from coming to accomplish his will.

W. Robertson Smith, Lectures on the Reli.a: Smith places magic among the private concerns of the individual, which ancient states treated as offenses against morals and the state. He says the suppression of magical rites was among the first priorities of a founder of a kingdom, and that Israel's law matches that of other well-ordered communities. Magic appears as the art of constraining demonic powers, and magical superstitions are said to invade tribal religion in times of social dissolution.

q.t: In better times, the religion of the tribe or state has nothing in common with the private and foreign superstitions or magical rites that raw fear might dictate to an individual. Religion is not an arbitrary relationship between an individual person and a supernatural power; it is a relationship of all the members of a community to a power that has the good of the community at heart and protects its law and moral order.

The simplest proof of this is that magic and sorcery, although they lay outside of religion and were forbidden arts in all the civilized states of antiquity, were yet never regarded as mere imposture. It was not denied that there were supernatural agencies at work in the world of which public religion took no account.

If supernatural help was sought for such things, it had to be sought through magical ceremonies designed to purchase or force [original: "constrain"] the favor of demonic powers with which the public religion had nothing to do. Not only did these magical superstitions exist outside of religion, but in all well-ordered states, they were regarded as illegal [original: "illicit"].

A. B. Ellis, The Ewe-Speaking Peoples of.a: A. B. Ellis reports that among the Ewe-speaking peoples the vō-sesao, or amulets, belong to particular gods and have no indwelling spirit. Priests alone know how to make them, and no prayers or sacrifices are offered to them. He lists magic powders that open doors, madden an enemy, or destroy sight, and ointments (iro) from priests that compel a person to lend money or to hear amorous proposals. He adds that divination is a priestly function done by throwing objects on the ground and reading how they fall, and he records omens such as the crowing of roosters at night.

q.t: Magic powders are very numerous. One kind, when blown against a door or window, causes it to fly open, no matter how securely it may be fastened; another, when thrown upon the footprints of an enemy, makes him go mad; a third, used in the same way, neutralizes the evil effects of the second; and a fourth destroys the sight of anyone who looks upon it.

These vō-sesao are believed to owe their power to being consecrated to, or belonging to, the gods, and the special property of a vō-sesa does not depend on an indwelling spirit. They enable the god to recognize and protect his people, just as the blood on the doorposts of the Jews enabled their God to recognize their homes when the firstborn in Egypt were slain (Exodus xii. 13).
Divination is a function peculiar to the priests and is usually performed by throwing objects on the ground and drawing inferences from the position in which they fall.
sympathetic magic is one of the earliest means by which man endeavours to adapt the agencies of nature to his needs.

The Namaquas abstain from eating the flesh of hares, because they think it would make them faint-hearted as a hare. But they eat the flesh of the lion, or drink the blood of the leopard or lion to get the courage and strength of these beasts.
The epilepsy is believed to have passed into the leaves, and to have been thrown away with them.

kb.t: J. G. Frazer, The Golden Bough
kb.th: Frazer treats sympathetic magic as one of the earliest means by which man tries to adapt nature to his needs, older than the worship of game animals.
h: Hunters used sympathetic magic before they worshipped game, and sympathetic magic is 'one of the earliest means' by which man adapts nature to his needs ([p. 144](/book/69907cd85f855ec553e77a81?page=144)).

Eating an animal is believed to pass on its qualities: the Zaparo avoid heavy meats lest they become unwieldy, and the Namaquas avoid hare lest they become faint-hearted ([p. 96](/book/69907cd85f855ec553e77a81?page=96)).

In the 'transference of ills', a disease is believed to pass into a leaf, stick or animal that is then thrown away or beaten, as when epilepsy is passed into leaves ([p. 159](/book/69907cd85f855ec553e77a81?page=159)).
an: Doutté rejects Frazer's picture of early magic as a 'false science', holding that the 'primitive' lacks the idea of an invariable link of cause and effect and that magic is a practice 'felt rather than perceived' ([p. 321](/book/69908a6393003de39c96519b?page=321)).

Catharine Cook Smith (1930) argues that Frazer lends the sorcerer his own logical premise, so that the magician comes out as a failed scientist or a wilful deceiver ([p. 14](/book/6ab22cdd277b509c83e964ad?page=14)).

Westermarck (1926) accepts Frazer's distinction and says magic deals with 'impersonal forces' and seeks control or constraint, coercing spirits when it addresses them ([p. 60](/book/6990794eb621b177c1af6190?page=60)).

James Mooney, The Sacred Formulas of the.a: Mooney reports that the Cherokees attribute disease and death to animal spirits, ghosts, or witches, and that the spirit of a plant can suggest the remedy to a doctor. Witches hasten the death of the sick to take the time left to them, and the Raven Mocker is the most dreaded. A shaman who wants to kill takes the victim's spittle, which gives power over that life, and sets it in a tube of wild parsnip with seven earthworms and splinters from a lightning-struck tree.

q.t: Like most primitive people, the Cherokees believe that disease and death are not natural, but are instead due to the evil influence of animal spirits, ghosts, or witches.

Possession of the man's spittle gives him power over the life of the man himself. Many ailments are said by the doctors to be caused by an enemy who has, by this means, "changed the spittle" of the patient, causing it to breed animals or sprout corn within the sick man's body.

The witch's goal in doing this is to prolong their own life by stealing whatever time they can take from the sick person. Because of this, a witch who is successful in these practices can live to be very old.

the presence of it is ascertained by proof. A man comes by chance upon a stone which takes his fancy; its shape is singular, it is like something, it is certainly not a common stone, there must be mana in it.

certain forms of words, generally in the form of a song, have power for certain purposes; a charm of words is called a mana. But this power, though itself impersonal, is always connected with some person who directs it

That invisible power which the natives believe causes all effects beyond their understanding of the natural world is generally known as mana. This power resides in spiritual beings, whether in the souls of living people or in the ghosts of the dead. It is passed on by them to their names and to various objects belonging to them, such as stones, snakes, and indeed things of all sorts.

kb.t: Robert Henry Codrington, The Melanesians
kb.th: Codrington describes Melanesian mana as a power outside the common processes of nature, known by its results and always tied to a person who directs it.
h: Mana is a power outside the common processes of nature whose presence 'is ascertained by proof' ([p. 148](/book/69a552fa0aade5c1d01fe786?page=148)).
A stone resembling a fruit is buried in the garden, and a good crop shows it has mana ([p. 148](/book/69a552fa0aade5c1d01fe786?page=148)).
The power, 'though itself impersonal, is always connected with some person who directs it' ([p. 148](/book/69a552fa0aade5c1d01fe786?page=148)).
tr: Mana names the power itself, and a charm of words is also called a mana ([p. 148](/book/69a552fa0aade5c1d01fe786?page=148)).

q.t: receive one hundred blows with the long stick … twenty ounces of silver … These laws can boast of a respectable age, as we find them in the Code of the Ming dynasty
both dynasties considered k u to be the most common and typical mode of poisoning.

sufferers from fever or other demoniacal diseases eat cakes of flour on which schoolmasters or other men of letters have written exorcising characters … A still more effective medicine for such patients is water in which a charm has been steeped or boiled, or which is mixed with ashes of a burnt charm.
THE WU WERE POSSESSED BY SPIRITS OR GODS.

kb.t: J. J. M. de Groot, The Religious System of China
kb.th: De Groot documents Chinese sorcery largely through the law and the state: poison-sorcery punished by the dynastic codes, and sorcery named as the harmful part of what the orthodox called heterodox.
h: De Groot quotes the Qing Code on gu poison-sorcery: the breeder's household is banished for life, a village chief who failed to report gets a hundred blows, and an informer is rewarded, with the same terms in the Ming Code ([p. 417](/book/69907970b621b177c1af72d1?page=417)).

Both the Ming and Qing dynasties held gu to be the most common and typical mode of poisoning, with kinds of snakes, geese, babies and gold caterpillars ([p. 418](/book/69907970b621b177c1af72d1?page=418)).

At Amoy, sufferers from demoniacal fevers ate cakes written with exorcising characters, and water steeped with a charm or mixed with its ashes was a stronger medicine ([p. 149](/book/69907973b621b177c1af7880?page=149)).
De Groot heads his chapter on the wu as spirit-mediums possessed by spirits or gods ([p. 292](/book/69907973b621b177c1af7880?page=292)).

In the wu-gu affair of 91 BCE, wu were employed to detect sorcerers suspected of attacking Emperor Wu's health, and princesses, the empress's kin and a minister were put to death ([p. 302](/book/69907973b621b177c1af7880?page=302)).
tr: Chinese books name sorcery yao or xie 'methods of demonry'; since xie covers everything contrary to the Tao, the terms also take in harmless heterodox rites and juggling, and de Groot treats sorcery as the harmful subset of heterodox practice ([p. 369](/book/69907970b621b177c1af72d1?page=369)).

Wu names a ritual office, and in the 91 BCE affair it names both the specialists who hunted sorcerers and the sorcery they hunted ([p. 292](/book/69907973b621b177c1af7880?page=292)); ([p. 302](/book/69907973b621b177c1af7880?page=302)).

k.g: the subtle, non-physical plane of existence
the practice of rituals to influence divine beings
the applied side of magical science

q.t: Magic is: the APPLICATION OF DYNAMIZED HUMAN WILL TO THE RAPID EVOLUTION OF THE LIVING FORCES OF NATURE.
all of this is only interesting as translations into a crude language of laws and ideas

Pantacular figures therefore have a value in ceremonial magic, and the Urim and the Thummim of the Jews, no more than the Christian host, which are talismans, escape this rule, as worship is, most often, only a magical ceremony misunderstood by the assistants as much as by the operator.

kb.t: Papus, Elementary Treatise on Practical Magic (Traité élémentaire de magie pratique)
kb.th: Papus defines magic as the human will, dynamised, applied to speeding the evolution of nature's living forces.
h: Magic is the application of dynamised human will to the rapid evolution of the living forces of nature ([p. 33](/book/695932b8b91a6184ea943faf?page=33)).

Papus tells the student that the visible world matters only as a translation, into a crude language, of laws and ideas the brain must extract from sensation ([p. 23](/book/695932b8b91a6184ea943faf?page=23)).

Where Agrippa's De vanitate reports the magi placing power in things themselves, graded up to celestial and intelligible things, Papus places the operative power in the operator ([p. 382](/book/69bd9ca46120d54bd037001f?page=382)).

k.g: a collection of hymns and spells

q.t: In a vast majority of cases, the magician seeks to achieve his goal by warding off demons or magical substances from himself or others; in another group of cases, he does so by directing them toward himself or others.

[Just as the speaking] of the name exerts a magical power over the named being, the naming of a desired process brings about the process itself, thanks to the same mystical bond between name and thing.
On the contrary, anyone who could used magic, and on every occasion. This does not mean that every practice was considered lawful.

kb.t: Hermann Oldenberg, The Religion of the Veda (Die Religion des Veda)
kb.th: Oldenberg argues that in Vedic practice magic and sacrifice were two procedures that mixed early, each drawing on the other.
h: Magical acts came to resemble or combine with sacrifices, and magic's mode of action was transferred to the sacrifice ([p. 331](/book/69907c815f855ec553e75cd5?page=331)).
The sacrificial setting, saturated with ideas of divine proximity and mysterious success, invited sorcery like no other ([p. 331](/book/69907c815f855ec553e75cd5?page=331)).
an: Bloomfield's reading of the same ritual texts finds witchcraft blended with every sphere of religious thought from the start, which tells against Oldenberg's two-procedure model ([p. 43](/book/69907c2f5f855ec553e71f1b?page=43)).

William Crooke, Religion and Folklore of.a: Crooke separates the harmless or benevolent magic (sympathetic, homeopathic and contagious) from black magic used for anti-social ends. He quotes Sir A. Lyall on the witch, who claims occult faculties of their own, and names tribes and castes with a reputation for sorcery. The exorcist, called Syāna, Sokha or Ojha, uses Mantras to make a familiar Bhūt drive off the spirit that causes illness.

q.t: First is the Mantra or spell. While properly a Vedic text, the term now extends to all magical forms of words, letters, sounds, or any "hocus-pocus" meant to bring good luck to the possessor and evil to their enemies, spirits, or those who cast the Evil Eye.

Black magic, as it is popularly called, is of a different type: it is employed for anti-social ends, for evil purposes such as the destruction of an enemy, the promotion of quarrels, and the like. The witch or warlock who practices it claims to effect his purpose by gaining control of some evil spirit whom he forces to obey him.

Exorcism of the spirits that bring disease upon men or animals has become a regular profession among the peasantry. The methods are magical, of the homeopathic or sympathetic type, and the exorcist is usually not a Brahman, but a member of one of the lower castes who, as original owners of the soil, are supposed to understand spirits and their ways.
Magic, and this mostly of a sympathetic kind, seems to have crept into Indian Buddhism soon after Buddha's death.

This is clearly a trick performed through sleight of hand using the multicolored ribbons attached to the arrow. However, it is regarded as a miracle, and the patient is led to believe that the demon has been sucked out of that part of the body.

Their deep-seated [original: "inveterate"] craving for physical protection against these harmful [original: "malignant"] gods and demons has led them to place their faith in charms and amulets. These can be seen everywhere, hanging from the clothing of every man, woman, and child.

kb.t: L. Austine Waddell, The Buddhism of Tibet, or Lamaism
kb.th: Waddell tells a story of decline in which magic, mostly of a sympathetic kind, crept into Buddhism soon after the Buddha's death and shaped its later ritual.
h: Magic 'mostly of a sympathetic kind' crept into Indian Buddhism soon after the Buddha's death ([p. 512](/book/69a5529b1e2c2347112f0ea1?page=512)).
Waddell cites irdhi, supernatural power, as an attribute of Arhats ([p. 512](/book/69a5529b1e2c2347112f0ea1?page=512)).
He treats the Paritta ('pirit') rite as essentially exorcism ([p. 512](/book/69a5529b1e2c2347112f0ea1?page=512)).
tr: Tibetan Buddhist sources count the wrathful rite (drag, abhicāra) as the fourth of four sanctioned activities, done after offerings and with the gurus' permission, so it has no place in an outlaw sense of 'magic' ([p. 319](/book/69e7aac85f1a22ab19a8d43f?page=319)); ([p. 412](/book/6abe9bd76a920ffd924d8fdc?page=412)).
an: Woodroffe objects that calling tantric mantra gibberish is an outsider's judgement, which tells against Waddell-style readings of lamaist mantra rites as charlatanism ([p. 518](/book/6a0f06e2900fb4799cef2aa4?page=518)).

H. A. van Hien, The Javanese Spirit Worl.a: Van Hien lists the devils that serve sorcerers and doekoen when called by formulas. The Madam's include cow-shaped ones used for revenge and four kinds tied to fire, earth, water, and air, which deceive bystanders and perform tasks in their element. His djampe formulas invoke Allah and the Prophet, include spells to bewitch and to lift bewitchment, and carry his warning that experiments can harm the experimenter.

q.t: The so-called Madam's are very undeveloped devils, which have the shape of a cow. They are used by malicious sorcerers and doekoen's traditional healers/shamans for carrying out plans of revenge.

Due to the various procedures that must be observed for these djampe's and others, we advise no one to experiment with these or other formulas, as those experiments can sometimes turn out to the disadvantage of the experimenter.

Stanislas de Guaita, The Key of Black Ma.a: Guaita names the Astral Light, or Universal Plastic Mediator, as the substantial force that sorcerers put to work for their malevolence, and says the adept can constrain it. He describes the will as the agent in every magical work. A sorcerer who gives up the will to larvae and lemures becomes their slave, and the law of the choc en retour strikes the one who works evil. He also notes that medieval physicists filed surprising discoveries under natural magic.

k.g: the cosmic medium or plastic mediator
the astral light of the sorcerers

q.t: It is a power unconscious in itself, but suited to reflecting all thoughts. It is an impersonal Power, yet capable of assuming all personalities. It is an invasive and dominating Power, which the adept can nevertheless penetrate, constrain, and subjugate.

We would have much to do if we had to research the magical use of the Will everywhere it plays a role, since there is no work, whether of light or of darkness, where it does not intervene: sometimes to exercise its empire (as the adepts proceed), and sometimes to abdicate it for the benefit of Larvae malicious astral entities and lemures restless spirits of the dead (of which the sorcerer eventually becomes the slave).

When physicists decided to publish some surprising recipe, being little interested in harvesting the small change of a reputation as nigremans practitioners of black magic or necromancy at the stake, they took care to catalog their discovery under the heading of natural magic the study of the hidden powers within nature, or occult physics the study of unseen natural forces.
IN all matters of ceremonial the inspiration of the Grimoires must be sought in the Key of Solomon proper, but for the names and offices of the demons it must be sought in the Lesser Key.

The date specified in the title of the Grimorium Verum is undeniably fraudulent; the work belongs to the middle of the eighteenth century, and Memphis is Rome. The "Grand Grimoire" is not of higher antiquity.

The oldest codex used by the English editor is in contracted Latin, and belongs to the sixteenth century. … It is, however, claimed that the work was written originally in Hebrew. In this claim there is nothing essentially improbable
There are two kinds of pacts, says the Grimorium Verum, the tacit and the manifest

kb.t: A. E. Waite, The Book of Black Magic and of Pacts / The Book of Ceremonial Magic
kb.th: Waite maps the ceremonial magic of the grimoires as a bibliographer, sending readers to the Solomonic keys while treating the books' claimed antiquity and authorship with suspicion.
h: Waite directs the reader to the Key of Solomon for ceremonial and to the Lemegeton for the names and offices of the demons ([p. 150](/book/69a552811e2c2347112f097f?page=150)).

He reports the Key of Solomon in Latin, French, Italian and German manuscripts, the oldest sixteenth-century Latin, and finds a Hebrew original not 'essentially improbable' ([p. 81](/book/69c896426c6f3cc53c85c4ea?page=81)).
He judges the Grimorium Verum's printed date 'undeniably fraudulent', placing it and the Grand Grimoire in the mid-eighteenth century ([p. 103](/book/69c896426c6f3cc53c85c4ea?page=103)).
He names back-dating and imputed authorship 'the two crying bibliographical sins of Grimoires' ([p. 49](/book/69c896426c6f3cc53c85c4ea?page=49)).

He repeats the Grimorium Verum's division of pacts into tacit and manifest, noting that Catholic theologians extended the pact to cover any communication with spirits ([p. 259](/book/69c896426c6f3cc53c85c4ea?page=259)).

Andrew Lang, The Making of Religion|||Hi.a: Lang cites reports that the primitive person explains prophecy and unlearned knowledge as possession by an outside spirit, a demon, ghost, or god. Some prophets are conscious frauds and others sincere, as in the missionary Dr. Mason's accounts of familiar spirits. He also describes divining sticks that move when a ghost's name is called, are guided by spirits among the Maori, and rise, fall, or jump among the Zulu.

q.t: The primitive person explains all these and similar phenomena with the hypothesis that an outside spirit—perhaps a demon, a ghost, or a god—has taken possession of the patient. The possessed person, being full of the spirit, delivers sermons, oracles, prophecies, and what Americans call "inspirational addresses," before returning to his normal consciousness.

Placed in a tree, it would lift them from the ground. In other cases, the holding of the sticks produces convulsions and trance.¹ The divining sticks of the Maori are also "guided by spirits,"² and those of the Zulu sorcerers rise, fall, and jump about.³

Baldwin Spencer and F. J. Gillen, The Na.a: Spencer and Gillen distinguish three schools of medicine men among the Arunta: those appointed by the Iruntarinia, those appointed by the Oruncha, and those initiated by other medicine men. They describe pointing sticks and bones (Injilla, Irna, Ullinka), charmed objects that cause wasting or blindness, and magic worked by women. They record that body-clipping magic is absent in these tribes, where human hair is a valued gift.

q.t: Individuals commonly called medicine men—though perhaps the terms magic men or wizards would be more accurate in certain respects—hold a very considerable influence within the tribe. Before dealing with their powers, we will first describe the way in which a man is admitted to the rank of medicine man.

We refer to the attempt to injure an enemy by obtaining and then performing a charm upon a part of their person, such as hair or nail clippings [this is often called "contagious magic"]. As we have already seen, images or representations of individuals are made with the idea that any hurt done to the image is felt by the person it represents through sympathy.

They remain in this position in perfect silence until they hear the Arungquiltha [original: Arungquiltha; a term used for both the evil magic and the spirit or essence residing within the ritual object], which in this instance is regarded as an evil spirit living in the magic tool, asking, “Where is he?”

Walter William Skeat, Malay Magic|||Sout.a: Skeat prints many invocations that address named spirits of sea, forest, river and bay, often closing with Islamic phrases such as "There is no God but God". The charms shown include crocodile charms, offerings to the sea spirits in the lanchang rite, and charms for laying the Pontianak, Penanggalan, Polong and Pelesit. He also describes familiar spirits such as the Bajang and the bracelet worn by children as protection against it.

q.t: While by divination and by inferences from omens and dreams, Malays attempt to ascertain the course of fate, so by charms of the nature of amulets and talismans they sometimes endeavor to influence its direction or modify its force.

Every act in their lives is regulated by some regard for the demons of the sea and air, and yet these folk are nominally Muhammadans, and, according to that faith, magic and sorcery, incantations to the spirits, and prayers to demons, are all unclean things forbidden to the people.
Thus, a Malay magician once told me that the Bajang took the form of a house-cricket, and that when thus embodied it may be kept by a man, just as the Pělěsit may be kept by a woman.

Joseph Hansen, Quellen und Untersuchunge.a: The collected texts show late medieval theologians explaining sorcery through demons and the pact. Geiler of Kaysersberg accounts for milk-stealing and night flight by the devil's power of local motion, and Wunschilburg treats spells and formulas as pacts of signs with demons. Hansen's own pages also set out the German and Latin words for magic and the terms used for witches.

q.t: The fork does not have this power from itself, nor does the ointment do it. Otherwise, if she anointed a little coat, that too would fly away. Therefore, it is the devil who does it.
Thus also these sorcerers do not obtain their results by the power of the words which they either speak or carry in writing, but by the honor they bestow upon the demons by speaking them.
Thus, demons and their disciples can stir up lightning, hail, and storms. They do this after receiving power from God, or His permission in the case of their disciples.
Where no apparatus is used, and the performance is shrouded in darkness, it is extremely difficult to prove trickery, however certain the investigator may be
The Fox girls are said to have taken no money for their performances at first, until indeed the "spirits" insisted on their doing so
evidence, such as we can regard as primâ facie worthy of consideration, for the exercise, by persons whose good faith may fairly be presumed, of any supernormal faculty, is almost entirely wanting

kb.t: Frank Podmore, Modern Spiritualism: A History and a Criticism
kb.th: Podmore's sceptical history of the séance finds evidence for any supernormal faculty, from persons of presumed good faith, 'almost entirely wanting' in early American spiritualism.
h: Evidence for any supernormal faculty from persons of presumed good faith is 'almost entirely wanting' in early American spiritualism ([p. 308](/book/69906a45d69de0e6980700d1?page=308)).

Trickery was seldom detected in early American spiritualism, and in darkened séances without apparatus fraud is extremely hard to prove even when the investigator is sure of it ([p. 308](/book/69906a45d69de0e6980700d1?page=308)).
The Fox sisters reportedly took no money at first, until the 'spirits' insisted, and money mattered less at early séances than later ([p. 310](/book/69906a45d69de0e6980700d1?page=310)).

q.t: the elementary obeys only through devotion or fear, but always remains free to resist the will of the Necromancer.

Stanislas de Guaita defined it very well: the implementation, for evil, of the occult forces of nature. While the magus exerts every effort to assist in the evolution of natural forces, the sorcerer, for his part, employs all his strength to paralyze the free expansion of evolutionary forces for the benefit of the forces of death and involution.

For occultists, spirits are divided into two primary broad sections: 1st, spirits inferior to human nature, called by the ancients "spirits of the elements," and by the moderns, since Paracelsus, elementals. These spirits are mortal, but can acquire immortality by rising to the level of human nature.

kb.t: Papus, Occultism and Spiritualism (L'Occultisme et le spiritualisme)
kb.th: Papus separates occultism from spiritism by the astral beings involved, distinguishing the elementaries a necromancer may call from the elementals of the astral fluids.
h: Elementaries obey a necromancer only through devotion or fear and always remain free to resist ([p. 58](/book/69593354b91a6184ea94486d?page=58)).
Elementals, unlike elementaries, circulate in the astral fluids ([p. 58](/book/69593354b91a6184ea94486d?page=58)).

Robert Hamill Nassau, Fetichism in West.a: Nassau separates a defensive 'white art' from an offensive 'black art' that he identifies with witchcraft, and judges both immoral because both use fetishes. He describes the magic doctor's rites, in which a spirit is invited into the patient or into a charm. He explains a failed charm as one whose spirit has died or been outmatched.

q.t: He admits that black magic is wrong because its goal is to kill or injure someone else. However, he thinks white magic is allowable because he uses it simply for defense.

According to the usual procedure, an article is prepared using incantations that refer to spiritual influences. This is worn by the applicant either as a cure for an existing disease or to protect against an expected danger.

He readily replies, "Yes, I know. You have an enemy who possesses a fetish containing a spirit more powerful than yours. This spirit made your bullet miss its mark and caused your opponent’s spear to wound you.

Frank Channing Haddock, Power of Will|||.a: Haddock states that the volumes of his Power-Book Library aim to be clear, plain, practical, sane, and helpful. He says he was conscious of neither chicanery nor suspicious "occultism" in mind, mood, or work.

q.t: The volumes of the Power-Book Library have sought always to be clear, plain, practical, sane, and helpful, and neither chicanery nor suspicious "occultism" has to the author been conscious in mind or mood or work.

Three Initiates, The Kybalion|||New Thou.a: The Three Initiates present Hermes Trismegistus as the source of occult wisdom, astrology and alchemy. They define 'Spirit' for occultists as living power or mystic force that can serve evil as well as good ends. They tie hypnotism and psychic phenomena to Suggestion, Vibration and Mental Gender.

q.t: He was known as Hermes Trismegistus [Greek for "Hermes the Thrice-Greatest."]. He was the father of the Occult Wisdom; the founder of Astrology; and the discoverer of Alchemy.

To occultists, the word "Spirit" is used to mean "the animating principle," carrying with it the idea of power, living energy, or mystic force. Occultists know that what they call "spiritual power" may be employed for evil as well as good ends (in accordance with the Principle of Polarity ), a fact recognized by most religions in their concepts of Satan, Beelzebub—

A correct understanding of Suggestion is necessary in order to intelligently comprehend the varied psychical phenomena which Suggestion underlies. But even more, a knowledge of Vibration and Mental Gender is necessary for the student of Suggestion.

With Frazer, Hubert and Mauss, Fossey, etc., we place magic at the base of religion, in the sense that for us, religion began by being essentially magical … for in the beginning, religion, like sorcery, was magic.
Magic is the domain of desire … Magic is a system of a priori … inductions carried out under the pressure of need by groups of individuals
Magic is therefore, above all, a technique; in many languages, the word used to designate it comes from a root meaning “to do” or “to act.”
Magic is, above all, originally a collective creation: it is the imagination of the entire clan at work

kb.t: Edmond Doutté, Magic and Religion in North Africa (Magie et religion dans l'Afrique du Nord)
kb.th: Doutté applies Hubert and Mauss to North African practice: magic is a technique of desire and a collective creation, and religion itself began as magic.
h: In the beginning religion, like sorcery, was magic, though a forbidden magic (sorcery) probably existed even then ([p. 345](/book/6990793c7d066daf3b4a9536?page=345)).
Magic is 'the domain of desire', a system of inductions made by groups under the pressure of need, and so above all a technique ([p. 320](/book/69908a6393003de39c96519b?page=320)).

Magic is originally a collective creation, and the magician exists as an individual only because his fellow tribesmen solicit and expect his acts ([p. 342](/book/69908a6393003de39c96519b?page=342)); ([p. 37](/book/695925eb15b4070cb1e7fe1f?page=37)).

Against Frazer and Jevons, magic is in its origins no 'false science', since the 'primitive' lacks the notion of invariable cause and effect and magic is 'felt rather than perceived' ([p. 321](/book/69908a6393003de39c96519b?page=321)).

His North African example of a wafq, a 4x4 square summing to 34, is cell for cell the 'table of Jupiter' Agrippa prints, and Dürer's Melencolia I square is the same square rotated and rearranged ([p. 299](/book/698420e1f1fb376a3d58061c?page=299)).
tr: Doutté notes that in many languages, Assyrian among them, the word for magic comes from a root meaning 'to do' or 'to act', while the Arabic words for magic come from different roots ([p. 320](/book/69908a6393003de39c96519b?page=320)).

Wallace D. Wattles, The Science of Getti.a: Wattles advises readers to keep away from Theosophy, Spiritualism and similar studies, and warns that dealings with the occult create mental cross-currents. He tells the reader to hold a clear mental image with faith and purpose, and to act on the present environment with full effort. He names projecting thought in a mysterious way as wasted effort.

q.t: Do not attempt to "project" your thoughts in any mysterious or occult [original: "occult" — here meaning supernatural, magical, or hidden from the natural senses.] way, with the idea that your mind will go out and do things for you. That is wasted effort and will weaken your ability to think with clarity and sanity.

If you begin to involve yourself with the occult [original: "occult" — supernatural or mystical practices.], you will create mental cross-currents [original: "mental cross-currents" — conflicting thoughts or mental distractions that counteract one's focused intention.] which will surely cause your hopes to be shipwrecked.

Do not try, by occult [original: "occult" — in this context, Wattles refers to hidden, esoteric, or "magical" mental attempts to influence others without physical action.] or mystical means, to act on people or things that are out of your reach.

Henri Doré, Researches into Chinese Supe.a: Doré describes Tantras as "manuals of magic" dedicated to different Bodhisattvas. Their aims include moving as fast as thought, invulnerability, the elixir of life, invisibility, making gold, defeating enemies, and conjuring spirits. Initiation by a master is a condition of success. Rosaries, amulets, lustral water, bells, and magic wands reinforce the formulas, and monks use incantations, finger movements, and processions to drive away bad stars. Door mirrors, arrows, trigrams, and tiger heads serve as talismans against harmful demons and bad influences, and a child's cap with silver characters opens the barrier of the revenant.

q.t: In summary, Tantras can be defined as "manuals of magic." Depending on the goal one wishes to reach, the books differ and are dedicated to different Bodhisattvas.

Whenever the number of years ends in 9, for example at 9, 19, 29, 39 years, etc., one must pass the barrier of the revenant. The child who has worn the four characters Koan-cha k'ai-t'ong barrier of the spirits opened on their cap will pass through it without difficulty and will not die.
Meaning: the mirror, Tchao-yao-king Zhaoyaojing; Demon-Finding Mirror, must reveal harmful demons.

Wallace Notestein, A History of Witchcra.a: Notestein says the Anglo-Saxon word "witch" meant someone who used spells and charms with the help of evil spirits. Early usage had no shape-changing, no pact with the Devil, no night meetings, and no systematic theology of demons. Citing Lea, he gives the later definition of a witch as one who renounced baptism and served Satan. A clear distinction between sorcery (spells or charms) and witchcraft (the diabolical pact) came in England much later. The statute under James made use of evil spirits the main proof of felony, so charging a woman with keeping a familiar was easier than charging murder.

k.g: The ritual calling upon or summoning of spirits or devils
The practice of calling upon or summoning spirits through rituals or spells
A contemporary term for forbidden arts like alchemy, astrology, or magic
People who use magic or rituals to gain secret knowledge or influence events
A folk remedy where a victim scratched the suspected witch to draw blood, which was believed to break the witch's spell

q.t: The word was the common term for someone who used spells and charms, and who was helped by evil spirits to achieve specific goals.

Certainly, a clear distinction between sorcery —the use of spells or charms—and witchcraft —the diabolical pact—was not made until much later, assuming that the lack of evidence to the contrary is a reliable guide.

Under the new statute, it was only necessary to prove that the woman made use of evil spirits, and she was put out of the way [executed]. It was a much simpler matter to charge a woman with keeping a "familiar" [original: "familiar"; a small animal or spirit believed to serve a witch] than to accuse her of murder.

Henri A. Junod, The Life of a South Afri.a: Junod holds that Black Magic and White Magic must be distinguished, and says the Thonga make this distinction with separate terms. Black magic is called Buloyi, the criminal practices of the baloyi (wizards or witches who work at night). When illness persists despite protective medicines, relatives consult a diviner who casts bones, including reedbuck or duiker ankle bones that stand for sorcerers. The bones are only a preliminary step, since no one accuses on their testimony alone, and the mungoma then "smells out" the noyi. The magicians' medicines serve protection and cure, and cure consists mainly of revealing the wizard.

k.g: a ritual gathering to identify witches

q.t: I believe that to avoid errors, it is vital to first clearly distinguish between Black Magic and White Magic. Although these adjectives, "black" and "white," are not used in this way among South African people, the Thonga certainly make this distinction and have different terms for each.
The patient's relatives visit a diviner, who will cast the bones to discover whether the disease is caused by witchcraft or not. This consultation is secret and serves only as a preliminary step.

All the power of the magicians is used to stop the enchantments of the baloyi. Their medicines are used for two purposes: protection and cure. The cure consists mainly of revealing the identity of the wizard.

J. G. Frazer, Folk-Lore in the Old Testa.a: Frazer holds that the magical influence of a written charm can be passed to a person who drinks the water it was washed into, a belief he calls widespread and ancient. He gives examples from Senegambia, Morocco, and North Africa, including formulas written on cakes, plates, and eggshells. He describes the magic mirror of water or ink, in which a diviner or boy professes to see persons living or dead and which is used to detect thieves. Of the witch of Endor, he suggests the voices of ghosts came from ventriloquism, which let the necromancer work without a confederate.

q.t: The notion, that the magical influence of a written charm, whether for good or evil, can be communicated to any person by making him or her drink the water into which the characters have been washed off, is widespread among superstitious people at the present time and has no doubt been so since the days of antiquity.

The diviner professes to see in the ink the figures of the persons, whether alive or dead, whom the inquirer desires him to summon up. The magic mirror of ink, like the magic mirror of water, is resorted to for the detection of a thief and other purposes.

Such audible effects could easily be produced by ventriloquism, which has the advantage of enabling the necromancer to work without the assistance of a confederate, and so to lessen the chance of detection.

incurred the charge of "gibberish," for such the Bījas sound to those who do not know what they mean. Though a Mantra such as a Bīja-mantra may not convey its meaning on its face, the initiate knows that its meaning is the own form (Svarūpa) of the particular Devatā
thus incurred the charge of "gibberish," for such the Bījas sound to those who do not know what they mean.
A Mantra is not the same thing as prayer or self-dedication ( Ātma-nivedana ). Prayer is conveyed in the words the Sādhaka chooses. Any set of words or letters is not a Mantra.

kb.t: John Woodroffe (Arthur Avalon), Shakti and Shakta
kb.th: Woodroffe sets out the tantric theory of mantra, in which each seed-syllable is the own-form of its deity and every mantra is a sound-form of Brahman. He rejects the outsider's charge that these syllables are gibberish.
h: Seed-syllables (bīja) such as hrīṃ, śrīṃ, krīṃ, hūṃ and phaṭ are, to the initiate, the own-form (svarūpa) of their deity ([p. 518](/book/6a0f06e2900fb4799cef2aa4?page=518)).
Every mantra is a particular sound-form of Brahman ([p. 518](/book/6a0f06e2900fb4799cef2aa4?page=518)).
Woodroffe calls the 'gibberish' charge against bīja-mantras an outsider's judgement, made by people who do not know what the syllables mean ([p. 518](/book/6a0f06e2900fb4799cef2aa4?page=518)).
Sādhanā is what produces siddhi, 'the result sought, be it material or spiritual advancement' ([p. 551](/book/6a0f06e2900fb4799cef2aa4?page=551)).
tr: Siddhi means attainment or success, worldly or liberating, and is no word for 'magic power' ([p. 551](/book/6a0f06e2900fb4799cef2aa4?page=551)).

Emma Curtis Hopkins, High Mysticism|||Ne.a: Emma Curtis Hopkins calls faith a kingship that commands, and names it the deepest secret of the Magia Jesu Christi. Faith is confidence to command the Working Executive in the universe, as Jacob heard "As a prince thou hast power with God, and hast prevailed." She presents Jesus teaching disciples to speak firmly and sternly to the Great Servant, by which insanity and poverty lose their grip.

q.t: For faith, which is kingship exercising to call the God of Lazarus to come forth, and the God of the withered arm to appear, is the deepest secret of all the deep secrets of the Magia Jesu Christi.

High faith is confidence to command the Working Executive standing up in the universe to the point of hearing as good response as Jacob, forebear of royal Jesus, heard: "As a prince thou hast power with God, and hast prevailed."
the church soon began to regard the practice of magic as foreign to the spirit of its religion. Thus the Thirty-sixth Canon of the Œcumenical Council held at Laodicea in 364 A.D.
Another widespread belief is that if a magician learns a person's name, he can gain magical power over them. This arose from the idea that a person's name was identical to the person themselves.

The Maklu, for example, contains eight tablets of incantations and spells against wizards and witches; the general idea throughout is to instruct the bewitched person how to manufacture figures of his enemies and thus destroy them.

kb.t: Lewis Spence, An Encyclopaedia of Occultism
kb.th: Spence's 'Magic' entry gives a short institutional history in which the early church came to regard magic as foreign to its religion.
h: The early church came to regard magic as foreign to its religion ([p. 303](/book/6953c85b77f38f6761bdc00b?page=303)).
Spence cites the thirty-sixth canon of the Council of Laodicea (364) as an instance of that church stance ([p. 303](/book/6953c85b77f38f6761bdc00b?page=303)).

k.g: a traditional group or assembly of witches, typically numbering thirteen

q.t: It can be traced back to pre-Christian times and appears to be the ancient religion of Western Europe.
caused Cotton Mather to say, 'The witches are organized like Congregational Churches.' This gives the clue at once.

The evidence proves that underlying the Christian religion was a cult practised by many classes of the community … It can be traced back to pre-Christian times and appears to be the ancient religion of Western Europe.

kb.t: Margaret Murray, The Witch-Cult in Western Europe
kb.th: Murray argues that the people called witches in late medieval times practised a pre-Christian religion of Western Europe, which she named the Dianic cult.
h: The people called witches practised a pre-Christian cult that was the ancient religion of Western Europe ([p. 16](/book/699069f01cf6ed5fbc8f4825?page=16)).
This 'Dianic cult' had organised rites and a horned or two-faced god ([p. 16](/book/699069f01cf6ed5fbc8f4825?page=16)).
Murray takes Cotton Mather's remark that the witches are 'organized like Congregational Churches' as 'the clue' to the cult's hierarchy ([p. 17](/book/699069f01cf6ed5fbc8f4825?page=17)).

Max Weber, Economy and Society (Wirtscha.a: Weber describes magic as the origin of divination, prayer and sacrifice. Spirits are an indefinite, material yet invisible something with a kind of will that lends effective power to objects, animals and people. The sorcerer is the permanently charismatically qualified person, set against the "layman", and holds ecstasy as the object of an "enterprise". Divination by omens can bind economic life, as with fung-shui geomancy, and prayer shades from magical formula into request, as in prayer wheels and rosaries.

k.g: a system of geomancy involving the arrangement of space to harmonize with spiritual forces

q.t: The art of "divination" grows initially directly from the magic of spirit belief. Spirits do not act, like all other beings, purely without rules. If one knows the conditions of their effectiveness, one can combine their behavior from symptoms: omina omens, which experience has shown indicate their disposition.
Naturally, the specific elements of "divine service"—prayer and sacrifice—are also initially of magical origin. With prayer, the boundary between magical formula and request remains fluid.
The sorcerer is the permanently charismatically qualified human in contrast to the everyday person, the "layman" in the magical sense of the term.
This is significant as hinting that Roman law did not condemn a man for magic unless he were proved to have committed some crime or made some unjust gain thereby.

My idea is that magic and experimental science have been connected in their development; that magicians were perhaps the first to experiment; and that the history of both magic and experimental science can be better understood by studying them together.

Magic is here understood in the broadest sense of the word, as including all occult arts and sciences, supersti- tions, and folk-lore. … The subject of laws against magic, popular practice of magic, the witchcraft delusion and persecution lie outside of the scope of this book.

The attempts of some of our authors to distinguish between magic and astrology, or magic and divination, or good and bad magic, or natural magic and sorcery, or witchcraft and counter-magic, have all been exceedingly illogical and unconvincing.

kb.t: Lynn Thorndike, A History of Magic and Experimental Science
kb.th: Thorndike argues that magic and experimental science were connected in their development, that 'magicians were perhaps the first to experiment', and that the two are better understood studied together.
h: Magic 'in the broadest sense' covers all occult arts, superstitions and folklore, though laws against magic, popular practice and the witch persecution fall outside the work and are left to Hansen ([p. 48](/book/699069212f82e0fda4804270?page=48)).

Neither spirits nor stars are always needed for magic; its sine qua non is 'a human operator, materials, rites, and an aim that borders on the impossible' ([p. 988](/book/699069252f82e0fda48046c3?page=988)).

Experimentation and magic were 'so constantly associated' in the period, yet 'the spirit of magic is different from the scientific spirit', since magic delights in the marvellous and casts credibility to the winds ([p. 991](/book/699069252f82e0fda48046c3?page=991)).
Magic declined, Thorndike suspects, because men came to set a greater value on truth, more than because it was shown false ([p. 989](/book/699069252f82e0fda48046c3?page=989)).

Thorndike reads Apuleius's Apology as hinting that Roman law condemned a man for magic only when he was shown to have done harm or gained unjustly by it ([p. 281](/book/699069212f82e0fda4804270?page=281)).
tr: Thorndike judges his medieval authors' efforts to separate magic from astrology or divination, good magic from bad, and natural magic from sorcery 'exceedingly illogical and unconvincing', and doubts there could be any magic but natural magic ([p. 988](/book/699069252f82e0fda48046c3?page=988)); ([p. 991](/book/699069252f82e0fda48046c3?page=991)).
an: Butler and Owen hold, against Thorndike's reading of Roman law, that the Twelve Tables had forbidden magic and that the law dealt with it adequately at every later period ([p. 176](/book/69af217f7c27d4b637fed9e0?page=176)).
Westermarck cites Thorndike for the medieval view that demons worked marvels largely through superior knowledge of the forces of nature ([p. 61](/book/6990794eb621b177c1af6190?page=61)).

q.t: Magic, on the other hand, deals with “impersonal forces” and aims at control or constraint, not conciliation.
The religious attitude is in its nature respectful and humble, the magical attitude is domineering and self-assertive.

the theologians mostly attributed the success of magic to demons, who were enticed by men to work marvels; but the demons were able to do so largely through their superior knowledge of the forces of nature.

kb.t: Edward Westermarck, Ritual and Belief in Morocco
kb.th: Following Frazer, Westermarck defines magic as dealing with impersonal forces and aiming at control or constraint, and he places its difference from religion in the practitioner's attitude.
h: Magic deals with 'impersonal forces' and aims at control or constraint, where religion seeks conciliation; when magic addresses spirits it coerces them ([p. 60](/book/6990794eb621b177c1af6190?page=60)).
The religious attitude is 'respectful and humble', the magical one 'domineering and self-assertive' ([p. 61](/book/6990794eb621b177c1af6190?page=61)).

Medieval theologians mostly credited magic's success to demons, but held that demons worked marvels largely through superior knowledge of the forces of nature, a point Westermarck takes from Thorndike ([p. 61](/book/6990794eb621b177c1af6190?page=61)).

G. L. Kittredge, Witchcraft in Old and N.a: Kittredge surveys English belief in charms, divination, crystal gazing, image magic and milk-stealing witchcraft, with medieval sermons and penitential writers condemning them. He notes that the English statute of 1542 penalizes incantation and witchcraft that harms persons or goods, and that Elizabethan English trials show no Witches' Sabbath. The notes list Old English legal and homiletic terms for witches, diviners and sorcery.

q.t: The common people, who brought the complaints, knew that some witch by her uncanny arts had killed or injured their cattle or their children or themselves, or had somehow damaged their property. The culprits confessed that they had familiar spirits in the shape of dogs and cats and toads. They admitted the practice of evil magic.
Do not put your trust in witchcraft. Whenever it seems true, it is merely through the devil’s craft to make men believe in what is hateful to God.
Trust not the chattering of a magpie—many men are deceived thereby; nor omens from a morning meeting, nor 'hansel' [a gift or omen marking the beginning of something], nor dreams.

AWARENESS of the living mystery—this defines the attitude of the magician. The priest, the holy man and the wizard, each seeks to awaken and to deepen the emotions that turn the minds of men towards the Irrational.

It may well be as some think that the elaborate directions for constructing the magic circle, calling the spirits and so on, had only a symbolic meaning and were really a form of words, a spell intended to bring about a certain state of mind in the magician and his followers.

The unconscious, the region of feeling, the region which we have called magic, uses in rites and symbols of all kinds another sort of language and this language is considered by the psycho-analysts to survive in dreams.

kb.t: Thābit ibn Qurra, On Images (De imaginibus)
kb.th: Thābit's book on images makes magic depend on astronomy: images gain their power by being made under the right constellations.
h: The work opens by stating that astronomy is needed in order to perform magic ([p. 711](/book/699069212f82e0fda4804270?page=711)).
Its images are to be made under prescribed constellations ([p. 711](/book/699069212f82e0fda4804270?page=711)).
an: An Arabic geomancy manual, the Ijtimāʿ al-shaml, names Thābit among the masters who verified how to compose names from letters assigned to the four natures and the lunar mansions (p. 89).

kb.t: William of Auvergne, On Laws (De legibus) and On the Universe (De universo)
kb.th: William of Auvergne treats demons as real agents able to move bodies and objects, and sets beside them wonders done through knowledge of the occult virtues of things.
h: William discussed demons tossing sticks and stones, throwing people from bed, and carrying men or rocks great distances ([p. 373](/book/699069252f82e0fda48046c3?page=373)).
He also discussed wonders done by those who know the occult virtues of things ([p. 373](/book/699069252f82e0fda48046c3?page=373)).
an: A text of c. 1412–1415 cites William as denying that the 'horse' on which evil spirits carry someone swiftly is a real horse ([p. 99](/book/69905e1a2fd6a039938a0f5d?page=99)).

kb.t: Arnald of Villanova, On Seals (De sigillis)
kb.th: Arnald's treatise on seals, as Thorndike reports it, treats astrological seals as engraved objects made to precise directions.
h: Arnald wrote a treatise on seals that gives directions for engraving them ([p. 872](/book/699069252f82e0fda48046c3?page=872)).
Thorndike reports that Arnald made Pope Boniface VIII an astrological seal in the form of a lion for his stone ([p. 872](/book/699069252f82e0fda48046c3?page=872)).
